q: Which list correctly states the Air Force core values?
o: Integrity First, Service Before Self, Excellence in All We Do
Integrity First, Service Before Self, Excellence Always
Duty, Honor, Country
Mission First, People Always, Excellence in All We Do
why: The three core values are Integrity First, Service Before Self, and Excellence in All We Do — the universal standard used to evaluate the ethical climate of all USAF organizations.

q: AFH 1 distinguishes values from ethics. How does it define ethics?
o: The systematic reflection of moral values that enables us to live and act according to our beliefs
A written code of punishable offenses under the UCMJ
The personal opinion of a commander applied to a situation
The set of customs enforced by the First Sergeant
why: Moral values describe what we hold to be right and wrong; ethics is the systematic reflection of those values enabling us to live and act according to our beliefs.

q: What is an ethical dilemma?
o: A situation where you are forced to choose between at least two alternatives
Any situation requiring a commander's decision
A violation of the UCMJ that carries punitive action
A disagreement between two Airmen about standards
why: An ethical dilemma is a situation where one is forced to choose between at least two alternatives. It is not automatically a legal violation.

q: Which three items are identified as the general causes or sources of ethical dilemmas?
o: Uncertainty, competing values, and potential harm
Greed, laziness, and dishonesty
Rank, authority, and seniority
Time pressure, fatigue, and resources
why: The three general causes are uncertainty, competing values, and potential harm.

q: Uncertainty as a source of ethical dilemmas results from which of the following?
o: Not having all the facts, not having enough experience, or not having a clearly established policy
Having too many competing regulations to read
A commander who refuses to issue guidance
Operating in a deployed environment
why: Uncertainty results from not having all the facts, not having enough experience, or not having a clearly established policy, procedure, or rule to follow.

q: Who presented the Airman's Creed to the Air Force, and in what year?
o: General T. Michael Moseley, 18th Chief of Staff, in 2007
General David Flosi, 20th Chief of Staff, in 2024
Secretary of the Air Force, in 1999
General Henry H. Arnold, in 1947
why: General T. Michael Moseley, 18th Air Force Chief of Staff, presented the creed in 2007 to reinvigorate the Total Force and build a warrior ethos.

q: Which regulation establishes the basic ethical principles and guidelines that must be followed by every government employee?
o: Title 5, CFR, Part 2635, Standards of Ethical Conduct for Employees of the Executive Branch
DAFMAN 36-2806
AFH 1, Chapter 19
why: Title 5, CFR, Part 2635 establishes the basic ethical principles and guidelines that every government employee must follow.

q: How long is the Chief of Staff of the Air Force appointed for, and by whom?
o: Four years, appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate
Two years, appointed by the Secretary of Defense
Four years, elected by the Air Staff
Indefinitely, appointed by the Secretary of the Air Force
why: The CSAF is a USAF General Officer appointed for four years by the U.S. President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.

q: Who is the head of the Department of the Air Force, and to whom is that position subject?
o: The Secretary of the Air Force, subject to the authority, control, and direction of the Secretary of Defense
The Chief of Staff of the Air Force, subject to the President
The Secretary of Defense, subject to Congress
The Vice Chief of Staff, subject to the CSAF
why: The SecAF is the head of the Department of the Air Force and is subject to the authority, control, and direction of the Secretary of Defense.

q: What is a Component MAJCOM (C-MAJCOM)?
o: The type of MAJCOM that is the USAF Component to a unified combatant command
A MAJCOM that has been placed in reserve status
A MAJCOM made up only of civilian employees
A MAJCOM that reports directly to the Secretary of the Air Force
why: A C-MAJCOM is the type of MAJCOM that serves as the USAF Component to a unified combatant command.

q: How is a Numbered Air Force (NAF) described?
o: An administrative level of command directly under a MAJCOM
The lowest level of command in the USAF
A joint command led by another service
A command equivalent to a wing
why: The NAF is an administrative level of command directly under a MAJCOM.

q: What is the minimum adjusted population a wing will have?
o: At least 1,000 (750 for Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Command)
At least 500 for all components
At least 2,500
At least 1,500 with no component exception
why: Wings have a minimum adjusted population of at least 1,000 — 750 for ANG and AFRC — including manpower authorizations, students, and a percentage of contractor workforces.

q: Where is Air Combat Command (ACC) headquartered, and when was it activated as a MAJCOM?
o: Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia; 1 June 1992
Scott Air Force Base, Illinois; 1 June 1992
Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana; 7 August 2009
Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio; 1 July 1992
why: ACC was activated as a MAJCOM on 1 June 1992 and is headquartered at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia.

q: Air Force Materiel Command (AFMC) is headquartered at which location?
o: Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio
Robins Air Force Base, Georgia
Hurlburt Field, Florida
Ramstein Air Base, Germany
why: AFMC was activated as a MAJCOM on 1 July 1992 and is headquartered at Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio.

q: Air Mobility Command (AMC) is headquartered at which installation?
o: Scott Air Force Base, Illinois
Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii
Joint Base San Antonio-Randolph, Texas
Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Virginia
why: AMC was activated as a MAJCOM on 1 June 1992 and is headquartered at Scott AFB, Illinois.

q: Which four areas make up the Airman Leadership School (ALS) curriculum?
o: Mission, leadership, problem solving, and USAF culture
Mission, discipline, drill, and heritage
Leadership, management, doctrine, and joint operations
Mission, fitness, customs, and finance
why: The ALS curriculum includes (1) mission, (2) leadership, (3) problem solving, and (4) USAF culture.

q: The NCO Distance Learning course consists of which three course modules?
o: Course foundation, leadership and management, and operational Airman
Mission, doctrine, and joint warfighting
Self-awareness, followership, and supervision
Foundation, culture, and fitness
why: The NCO-DL course consists of three modules: course foundation, leadership and management, and operational Airman.

q: Which statement about EPME Distance Learning Course (DLC) completion is correct?
o: DLC completion is no longer a prerequisite for resident attendance, effective 26 April 2018
DLC completion has always been required before resident attendance
DLC completion is required only for the Chief Leadership Course
DLC completion is required only for Air National Guard members
why: EPME Distance Learning Courses completion is no longer a prerequisite for resident attendance effective 26 April 2018.

q: Enlisted Joint PME (EJPME) II is focused on preparing which members?
o: E-7 through E-9 for senior leadership roles in joint assignments
E-4 through E-6 for their first supervisory role
E-1 through E-3 for upgrade training
Civilian employees only
why: EJPME II is focused on preparing E-7/E-9 enlisted members for their senior leadership roles in joint assignments.

q: What must students do before enrolling in EJPME?
o: Complete rank-required service enlisted PME
Complete an associate degree
Obtain a joint duty assignment
Complete the Chief Leadership Course
why: Students must complete rank-required service enlisted PME before enrolling in EJPME.

q: In what year were enlisted PME schools established across the USAF?
why: In 1955, enlisted PME schools were established across the USAF to give NCOs the leadership and management training needed for day-to-day mission execution.

q: Which statement about collegiate credit for enlisted PME is correct?
o: With the exception of the Chief Leadership Course, Airmen are awarded CCAF credit, which is accredited through Air University by SACSCOC
No enlisted PME course awards collegiate credit
Only the Chief Leadership Course awards collegiate credit
Credit is awarded only after promotion to MSgt
why: Except for the Chief Leadership Course, Airmen earn collegiate credit through CCAF, accredited through Air University by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges.

q: What is the authorized average percentage of RegAF enlisted members in pay grades E-8 and E-9 in a fiscal year?
o: No more than 2.5 percent and 1.25 percent, respectively
No more than 3.0 percent each
No more than 1.25 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively
No more than 5 percent each
why: The authorized average of RegAF enlisted members in E-8 and E-9 in a fiscal year may not be more than 2.5 percent and 1.25 percent, respectively.

q: The Combat Action Medal is awarded to military members in which grades?
o: E-1 through O-6 who actively participated in ground or air combat on or after 11 September 2001
E-1 through E-9 only
O-1 through O-6 only
All grades with no restriction
why: The Combat Action Medal is awarded to grades E-1 through O-6 who actively participated in ground or air combat on or after 11 September 2001.

q: The Gallant Unit Citation was approved by the Secretary of the Air Force in which year?
o: March 2004
September 2001
June 1992
August 2009
why: The Gallant Unit Citation was approved by the SecAF in March 2004 for extraordinary heroism in action against an armed enemy on or after 11 September 2001.

q: The Afghanistan Campaign Medal recognizes service during which period?
o: 11 September 2001 to 31 August 2021
9 March 2003 to 31 December 2011
11 September 2001 to a future date to be determined
24 March 1999 to 31 December 2013
why: Established 29 November 2004, the Afghanistan Campaign Medal covers designated Afghanistan operations from 11 September 2001 to 31 August 2021.

q: The Air Reserve Forces Meritorious Service Medal is awarded for what service?
o: 4 continuous years on or after 1 April 1965, or 3 continuous years on or after 1 July 1975
2 continuous years in any status
10 continuous years of reserve service
5 continuous years on or after 11 September 2001
why: It recognizes exemplary behavior, efficiency, and fidelity in enlisted status in the ANG and AFR for 4 continuous years (on/after 1 Apr 1965) or 3 continuous years (on/after 1 Jul 1975).

q: Which publication outlines the Department of the Air Force Military Awards and Decorations Program?
o: DAFMAN 36-2806, Military Awards: Criteria and Procedures
DAFMAN 36-2664
AFH 1, Chapter 8
why: The program is outlined in DAFMAN 36-2806, Military Awards: Criteria and Procedures, which recognizes units, organizations, and individuals and fosters morale and esprit de corps.

q: According to DAFMAN 36-2664, how far in advance of the scheduled test date must promotion eligible Airmen have access to reference materials?
o: At least 60 days
At least 30 days
At least 90 days
At least 120 days
why: Promotion eligible Airmen must have access to reference materials at least 60 days before the scheduled test date.

q: Which statement about group study for enlisted promotion testing is correct?
o: Group study of two or more people for promotion testing purposes is strictly prohibited
Group study is permitted if led by an NCO
Group study is permitted off-duty only
Group study is encouraged by WAPS
why: Airmen must use a self-initiated program of individual study; group study (two or more people) for promotion testing is strictly prohibited.

q: Enlisted personnel who violate promotion test prohibitions are subject to prosecution under which article of the UCMJ?
o: Article 92
Article 134
Article 120
Article 15
why: Violators are subject to prosecution under Article 92 of the UCMJ for violating a lawful general regulation.

q: Which of the following is prohibited under AFH 1's promotion testing rules?
o: Sharing pretests, recalled test questions, personal study materials, highlighted references, or commercial study guides with others
Using official electronic study references on a government computer
Reviewing your DVR in PRDA
Taking leave to study
why: Sharing pretests or recalled questions, personal study materials, underlined or highlighted study references, and commercial study guides with other individuals is prohibited. Government computers may only be used to view official electronic references.

q: What is the Data Verification Record (DVR)?
o: The document used for promotion consideration and the most important tool to review for record completeness
A form used to request a test date change
A counseling form completed by the supervisor
The enlistment contract addendum for promotion
why: The DVR is the document utilized for promotion consideration and is the most important tool to review to ensure the promotion record is complete. It is reviewed in ARMS/PRDA.

q: What is the promotion eligibility cutoff date (PECD)?
o: The date promotion criteria are considered for promotion, used to determine eligibility and when selection folder data must be complete
The first day of the WAPS testing window
The date a member arrives at a new duty station
The date promotion results are released
why: The PECD determines promotion eligibility and is the cutoff for when selection folder contents and promotion evaluation brief data must be updated and complete.

q: Which publication contains the Enlisted Promotions References and Requirements Catalog (EPRRC)?
o: The EPRRC is the catalog that lists applicable study references Airmen must obtain for their cycle
It is AFH 1, Chapter 9, Attachment 2
It is the DVR generated in PRDA
It is DAFMAN 36-2664, Part Four
why: Eligible individuals must obtain all applicable study references as outlined in the EPRRC. The EPRRC is the WAPS catalog of study references for the cycle.

q: A member who will be unavailable during the entire testing cycle must do what?
o: Be prepared to test prior to departure, even if that is before the first day of the testing cycle
Request a waiver from AFPC after the cycle ends
Test during the supplemental cycle only
Transfer eligibility to the next promotion year
why: Members unavailable for the entire testing cycle must be prepared to test before they depart, even ahead of the official first day of the cycle.

q: Under the Blended Retirement System (BRS), how is retired pay calculated?
o: 2.0% times years of service times the average of the highest 36 months of base pay
2.5% times years of service times final basic pay
2.0% times years of service times final basic pay
2.5% times years of service times the highest 36 months of base pay
why: BRS applies to members who entered on or after 1 January 2018: 2.0% × YOS × average of the highest 36 months of base pay, with full CPI inflation protection.

q: Which retirement plan applies to members who entered service prior to 8 September 1980?
o: Final Basic Pay — 2.5% times years of service times basic pay
High-3 — 2.5% times years of service times the highest 36 months
BRS — 2.0% times years of service times the high-36
REDUX only
why: The Final Basic Pay plan uses 2.5% × YOS × basic pay for members who entered service prior to 8 September 1980.

q: A 30-year career is computed as 2% times 20 years plus 3.5% for the 10 years beyond 20. What is the maximum multiplier at 30 years?
why: That computation results in a maximum of 75% of the retired pay base at 30 years; service beyond 30 years adds 2.5% per year, up to 100%.

q: What are the maximum SGLI and FSGLI coverages described in AFH 1?
o: SGLI up to $500,000; FSGLI up to $100,000 for spouse and $10,000 for dependent children
SGLI up to $400,000; FSGLI up to $50,000 for spouse
SGLI up to $500,000; FSGLI up to $25,000 for spouse
SGLI up to $250,000; FSGLI up to $100,000 for spouse
why: SGLI provides up to $500,000 in life insurance; FSGLI provides up to $100,000 for a spouse and $10,000 for dependent children.

q: Enlisted members are eligible to retire with how much service?
o: 20 years of Total Active Federal Military Service, with no restrictions per DAFI 36-3203
15 years of TAFMS
18 years of active service with commander approval
20 years of total service including inactive time
why: Enlisted members are eligible to retire with 20 years of TAFMS and no restrictions per DAFI 36-3203, Service Retirements.

q: Where are legal services performed on an installation?
o: By the Office of the Staff Judge Advocate — not within Military & Family Readiness Centers
By the M&FRC legal assistance office
By the first sergeant
By the Inspector General
why: Legal services are not performed by or within M&FRCs; they are performed by the Office of the Staff Judge Advocate on the installation.

q: When personal status or family circumstances change requiring a DAF Form 357, members must notify their commander or first sergeant within what timeframe?
o: Immediately, or within 30 days (60 days for Selected Reserve)
Within 10 days for all components
Within 90 days
Within 45 days (15 days for Selected Reserve)
why: Members must notify their commander or first sergeant immediately, or within 30 days (60 days for Selected Reserve), if changes require completion of a DAF Form 357.

q: What is the Red Cross toll free number for service members and families in the United States?
why: AFH 1 lists the American Red Cross toll free number for service members and families in the U.S. as 1-800-733-2767.

q: The DoD budget program operates on a fiscal year basis covering which period?
o: 1 October through the following 30 September
1 January through 31 December
1 July through 30 June
1 April through 31 March
why: The budget program operates on a fiscal year basis from 1 October through the following 30 September.

q: The Future Years Defense Program (FYDP) is composed of how many major force programs?
o: 11 major force programs and over 3,600 active program elements
7 major force programs and 1,200 program elements
15 major force programs and 500 program elements
5 major force programs and 900 program elements
why: The FYDP is composed of 11 major force programs and over 3,600 active program elements used to categorize functional or organizational entities and their resources.

q: Which form is required documentation for investigating the loss, damage, destruction, or theft of government property?
o: DD Form 200, Financial Liability Investigation of Property Loss
DAF Form 357
SF 312
DD Form 1149
why: DD Form 200 documents the facts and circumstances of loss, damage, destruction, or theft and is required for financial liability investigations.

q: Who appoints a property custodian?
o: An accountable property officer, commander, or chief of staff agency
The unit first sergeant only
The base comptroller only
The member's supervisor
why: A property custodian is appointed by an accountable property officer, commander, or chief of staff agency and is directly responsible for physical custody, inventory, accounting, and reconciliation.

q: USAF program execution is reviewed during budget execution reviews in which months?
o: February, April (with the internal mid-year review), and July
January, June, and December
March, August, and November
October, January, and April
why: Program execution is reviewed in February, April (concurrent with the internal USAF mid-year review), and July.

q: How should emergency work requests be requested and accomplished?
o: By the quickest means possible, to include verbal or phone communication
Only through written DD Form 200 submission
Only through the unit's monthly work-order cycle
After the next budget execution review
why: Emergency work requests should be requested and accomplished by the quickest means possible, including verbal or phone communication.

q: How is transformational leadership defined?
o: A style of leadership defined by offering followers a vision and inspiring their mission
A style built on rank-based authority and compliance
A style focused solely on task proficiency
A style that trades rewards for performance
why: Transformational leadership is defined by the application of offering followers a vision and inspiring their mission.

q: What is inspirational motivation?
o: Leaders develop and articulate visions that paint an optimistic, enthusiastic, and inspiring picture of the future
Leaders reward followers who meet production goals
Leaders enforce standards through corrective action
Leaders delegate all vision-setting to subordinates
why: Inspirational motivation is when leaders develop and articulate visions that paint an optimistic and enthusiastic picture of the future that is appealing and inspiring to followers.

q: What is task power?
o: Power that stems from being good at a particular task and being able to help others with a process they are responsible for
Power granted by a commander's appointment letter
Power derived from controlling resources and budgets
Power earned through seniority and time in grade
why: Task power stems from being good at a particular task and being able to help others with a process or procedure they may be responsible for.

q: Why does AFH 1 emphasize self-awareness in leaders?
o: Self-aware leaders act consistently with their own values and are less likely to project their biases onto Airmen
Self-aware leaders are automatically promoted faster
Self-awareness replaces the need for feedback
Self-awareness is required for enlisted performance reports
why: Self-aware leaders are more likely to act consistently with their own values and actions and less likely to project their own biases onto Airmen.

q: How does AFH 1 describe charisma?
o: An energy emitted by leaders to inspire Airmen to perform a task when aspects of the mission are not intrinsically motivating
A personality trait that cannot be developed
The ability to enforce discipline without counseling
The authority to direct work by position alone
why: Charisma is an energy emitted by leaders to inspire Airmen to perform a task or objective when aspects of a mission are not intrinsically motivating or compelling.

q: How do effective leaders view failure?
o: As one of the greatest learning tools an organization has for achieving success
As something to be hidden from higher headquarters
As grounds for immediate removal from a position
As an unavoidable result of junior personnel
why: Leadership involves risks and rewards, and effective leaders realize failure is one of the greatest learning tools an organization has for achieving success.

q: Critical listening is best described as the sum of which two elements?
o: Informative listening and critical thinking
Empathic listening and note taking
Active listening and paraphrasing
Informative listening and nonverbal feedback
why: Critical listening is usually thought of as the sum of informative listening and critical thinking, because the listener is actively analyzing and evaluating the message.

q: When is empathic listening most appropriate?
o: When communication is emotional, or when the relationship matters as much as the message
When time is short and facts must be transmitted
When delivering formal briefings to senior leaders
When documenting a disciplinary action
why: Empathic listening is often useful when communication is emotional or when the relationship between speaker and listener is as important as the message — such as mentoring and counseling.

q: Which type of speech often includes humor and wit, such as a speech to entertain at a dining-out?
o: Entertaining speech
Informative speech
Persuasive speech
Ceremonial speech of instruction
why: Entertaining speeches often include humor and wit to entertain listeners, such as a speech to entertain at a dining-out.

q: How does AFH 1 define gestures?
o: The purposeful use of the hands, arms, shoulders, and head to reinforce what is being said
Unconscious movements that reveal nervousness
Any movement made while speaking
Hand movements used only in formal ceremonies
why: Gestures are the purposeful use of the hands, arms, shoulders, and head to reinforce what is being said. Purposeful body movement is free, yet deliberate.

q: Purposeful, effective body movement during a speech is best described as which of the following?
o: Free, yet deliberate movement
Constant motion to hold attention
Rigidly still posture
Movement timed to each sentence
why: AFH 1 describes purposeful, effective body movement as free, yet deliberate movement.

q: What is Step 3 of the Five-Step Risk Management Process?
o: Develop controls and make decisions
Identify the hazards
Assess the hazards
Supervise and review
why: Step 3 of the Five-Step Risk Management Process is to develop controls and make decisions.

q: The risk assessment matrix associated with Step 2 forms a risk assessment for each hazard by combining which two factors?
o: Probability of occurrence and severity
Cost and schedule
Frequency and duration
Manning and training
why: The risk assessment matrix combines the probability of occurrence with severity to form a risk assessment for each hazard.

q: In-depth risk management planning is normally reserved for which situations?
o: Complex operations and systems, and high priority or high visibility situations where hazards are not well understood or easily predictable
Routine daily tasks with known hazards
Any activity requiring a supervisor's signature
Only deployed operations
why: In-depth risk management is for complex operations and systems and high priority, high visibility situations where hazards are not well understood or easily predictable.

q: A job safety analysis is used in which situation?
o: To evaluate each work task not governed by a technical order or other definitive guidance, or when a new task or process is introduced
To evaluate tasks already covered by a technical order
Only after a mishap has occurred
Only for tasks performed by civilians
why: A job safety analysis evaluates tasks not governed by a TO or other definitive guidance, and when a new work task or process is introduced into the workplace.

q: How often do the principles of risk management apply?
o: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year, by all personnel for all on- and off-duty activities
Only during duty hours
Only during high-risk activities
Only when a supervisor directs
why: These principles are the cornerstones of effective risk management and apply 24/7/365 by all personnel for all on- and off-duty activities.

q: What two actions make up Step 5 of the Risk Management Process?
o: Supervising and monitoring the operation, and reviewing and evaluating to ensure risk and cost are in balance
Identifying hazards and assessing risks
Developing controls and making decisions
Implementing controls and re-briefing
why: Step 5 includes (1) supervising and monitoring the operation or activity and (2) reviewing and evaluating to ensure risk and cost are in balance.

q: What must be established to ensure corrective or preventative action taken was effective?
o: A feedback system
A mishap report
A risk assessment matrix
A safety bulletin board
why: A feedback system must ensure corrective or preventative action was effective and that newly discovered hazards are analyzed with follow-on corrective action.

q: Before granting access to classified information, a person must have which three things?
o: Security clearance eligibility, a signed SF 312, and a need-to-know
A CAC, a signed NDA, and a supervisor's approval
Security clearance eligibility, a badge, and an escort
Need-to-know, a briefing, and a background check
why: Access requires (1) security clearance eligibility, (2) a signed Standard Form 312, Classified Information Non-Disclosure Agreement, and (3) a need-to-know.

q: Unauthorized disclosure of which level of classified information could reasonably be expected to cause exceptionally grave damage to national security?
o: Top Secret
Secret
Confidential
Controlled Unclassified Information
why: Top Secret applies when unauthorized disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause exceptionally grave damage to national security.

q: Unauthorized disclosure of Secret information could reasonably be expected to cause what?
o: Serious damage to national security
Exceptionally grave damage to national security
Damage to national security
No damage to national security
why: Secret applies when unauthorized disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause serious damage; Confidential applies to damage.

q: Which cover sheet is used for Top Secret information outside of storage?
o: SF 703
SF 704
SF 705
SF 312
why: SF 703 is the Top Secret cover sheet, SF 704 the Secret cover sheet, and SF 705 the Confidential cover sheet. SF 312 is the non-disclosure agreement.

q: To be authorized to derivatively classify information within DoD, personnel must meet which training requirements?
o: Receive initial training before making derivative classification decisions and refresher training every year
Complete a single initial training course only
Receive refresher training every three years
Be a commissioned officer
why: All cleared DoD personnel are authorized to derivatively classify if they received initial training before making derivative classification decisions and refresher training every year.

q: What is a compromise in the security context?
o: A security incident (a violation) involving unauthorized disclosure of classified information to a person without valid clearance, access, or need to know
Any lost or misplaced document regardless of classification
A failed inspection of a classified storage area
An inadvertent public release of unclassified information
why: A compromise is a security violation in which there is unauthorized disclosure of classified information to persons without a valid clearance, authorized access, or need-to-know.

q: An authorized person who removes classified material from storage must do what?
o: Keep it under constant surveillance
Secure it in a locked desk drawer
Log the removal within 24 hours only
Notify the commander in writing before removal
why: An authorized person shall keep classified material removed from storage under constant surveillance.

q: When questioned, what information is a prisoner of war required by the Geneva Conventions to give?
o: Name, rank, service number, and date of birth
Name, unit, and mission
Name, rank, and home address
Name, rank, and names of fellow captives
why: When questioned, a POW is required by the Geneva Conventions and permitted by the UCMJ to give name, rank, service number, and date of birth.

q: Under the Code of Conduct, what is required of the senior prisoner of war?
o: Represent prisoners of war in matters of camp administration, health, welfare, and grievances
Approve all communications with captors
Assign work details to junior POWs
Determine punishments for camp infractions
why: The senior POW is required to represent POWs in matters of camp administration, health, welfare, and grievances.

q: AFH 1 distinguishes capture from evasion. Capture occurs when which conditions exist?
o: The member has no means to resist, evasion is impossible, and further fighting would lead to death with no significant loss to the enemy
The member is outnumbered and low on ammunition
The member is wounded and cannot walk
The member's unit has been ordered to withdraw
why: Capture occurs when a member has no means to resist, evasion is impossible, and further fighting would lead to death of the U.S. member with no significant loss to the enemy.

q: A prisoner of war who voluntarily informs or collaborates with the captor is subject to what?
o: Punishment under the UCMJ after repatriation as a traitor to the United States and fellow POWs
Immediate release by the captor
No consequence, since the Code of Conduct is not punitive
Administrative discharge only
why: A POW who voluntarily informs or collaborates with the captor is a traitor to the United States and fellow POWs, and after repatriation is subject to punishment under the UCMJ.

q: AFH 1 describes the Code of Conduct as which of the following?
o: A moral code providing a standard of conduct that all members are expected to measure up to
A punitive article of the UCMJ
An administrative instruction for deployed personnel
A treaty obligation under the Geneva Conventions
why: The Code of Conduct is a moral code designed to provide U.S. military personnel with a standard of conduct that all members are expected to measure up to.

q: The Equal Opportunity office must complete the informal complaint process within how many calendar days of filing?
o: 30 calendar days, unless the complainant grants an extension not to exceed 60 additional days
45 calendar days with no extension
60 calendar days with a 30-day extension
10 calendar days with a 20-day extension
why: The EO office must complete the informal complaint process within 30 calendar days unless the complainant grants an extension not to exceed 60 additional calendar days.

q: For a civilian formal EO complaint, initial contact must occur within how many calendar days of the alleged discriminatory matter?
o: 45 calendar days
30 calendar days
60 calendar days
180 calendar days
why: For the complaint to be processed at the formal stage, initial contact must be within 45 calendar days of the matter alleged to be discriminatory, or of the effective date of a personnel action.

q: How long does the EO office have to make a determination to accept, dismiss, or partially dismiss a formal complaint so an investigation can be completed?
o: 180 calendar days from the date filed
90 calendar days from the date filed
45 calendar days from the date filed
365 calendar days from the date filed
why: The EO office must process formal complaints expeditiously and determine whether to accept, dismiss, or partially dismiss within 180 calendar days from the date filed.

q: How does AFH 1 define fraternization?
o: An unprofessional relationship between an officer and enlisted member specifically prohibited by Article 134, UCMJ
Any personal relationship between two members of different ranks
A relationship between a supervisor and a subordinate
Dating within the same unit
why: Fraternization is an unprofessional relationship between an officer and enlisted member specifically prohibited by Article 134, UCMJ.

q: Formal complaints of sexual harassment are referred to which agency for an independent investigation?
o: Security forces, pursuant to 10 USC § 1561
The Equal Opportunity office
The Inspector General
The servicing legal office
why: Formal complaints of sexual harassment are referred to security forces for an independent investigation pursuant to 10 USC § 1561.

q: Who is the Victims' Counsel?
o: A military attorney authorized to provide independent legal representation to eligible victims of sexual assault, sexual misconduct, stalking, and similar crimes
A civilian advocate assigned by the SARC
The squadron first sergeant
A paralegal in the legal office
why: The Victims' Counsel is a military attorney authorized to provide independent legal representation to eligible victims.

q: Sexual assault encompasses offenses prohibited by which UCMJ articles?
o: Articles 120, 120b, and 80
Articles 92 and 134
Articles 128 and 128a
Articles 107 and 121
why: Sexual assault encompasses offenses prohibited by Articles 120, 120b, and 80, including rape, sexual assault, aggravated and abusive sexual contact, forcible sodomy, and attempts.

q: Under DoDI 6490.08, mental health providers are required to disclose which information to commanders?
o: Safety issues (suicidal or violent thoughts or self-injurious behavior) and fitness for duty issues
All counseling session notes
Any diagnosis of PTSD
Only information the member consents to release
why: Providers must disclose safety and fitness-for-duty issues to commanders; all other information is confidential.

q: What are the Air Force Medical Service's four primary objectives?
o: Promote and sustain a healthy and fit force, prevent illness and injury, restore health, and optimize human performance
Recruit, train, equip, and deploy medics
Treat, transport, document, and report
Prevent, protect, respond, and recover
why: The AFMS's four primary objectives are to promote and sustain a healthy and fit force, prevent illness and injury, restore health, and optimize human performance.

q: How does AFH 1 describe psychological first aid?
o: A way of reducing initial and ongoing stress by developing adaptive coping and recovery skills
A formal mental health diagnosis
A mandatory counseling session after deployment
A medical treatment administered only by providers
why: Psychological first aid reduces initial and ongoing stress by developing adaptive coping and recovery skills.

q: Which of the following are listed as signs of physical stress?
o: Frequent illness, headaches, high blood pressure, increased heart rate, physical exhaustion, sleep disturbances, or weight gain or loss
Only diagnosed medical conditions
Withdrawal from social activities and loss of interest
Increased motivation and focus
why: Physical stress can manifest as frequent illness, headaches, high blood pressure, increased heart rate, physical exhaustion, sleep disturbances, or weight change.

q: The redeployment support timeline identifies activities at which junctures?
o: Critical redeployment, recovery, reintegration, and reconstitution
Notification, deployment, tour, and return
Pre-deployment, mid-tour, and post-deployment
Train, deploy, employ, and redeploy
why: The redeployment support timeline identifies activities at the critical redeployment, recovery, reintegration, and reconstitution junctures.

q: Which aspect of readiness does AFH 1 emphasize in the deployment cycle?
o: Receiving continued support upon return from deployment
Completing pre-deployment training
Securing financial entitlements before departure
Arranging household goods shipment
why: While preparation, deployment, and post-deployment support are all important, receiving continued support upon return from deployment is an emphasized aspect of readiness.

q: In drill, what is an element?
o: The basic formation; the smallest drill unit, comprised of at least 3 individuals, usually 8 to 12, one of whom is the element leader
A formation of exactly four individuals
A unit of two or more flights
The largest drill unit in a squadron
why: An element is the basic formation and smallest drill unit — at least 3 individuals, usually 8 to 12, one designated as the element leader.

q: The three asymmetrical spires of the Air Force Memorial reach what heights?
why: The star is centered at the base of the three asymmetrical spires reaching heights of 201, 231, and 270 feet.

q: What is central to the Air Force Memorial and who created it?
o: A 16-foot bronze Honor Guard Statue created by sculptor Zenos Frudakis
A 20-foot granite eagle created by Felix de Weldon
A 12-foot bronze airman created by James Earle Fraser
A 16-foot marble statue created by Daniel Chester French
why: Central to the Air Force Memorial is the 16-foot bronze Honor Guard Statue, created by sculptor Zenos Frudakis.

q: Saluting recipients of the Medal of Honor is best described how?
o: Encouraged as a matter of respect and courtesy, though not required by law or regulation, and rendered regardless of rank or status
Required by regulation for all military members in uniform
Required only when in uniform and of junior rank
Prohibited unless the recipient is in uniform
why: Although not required by law or military regulation, members of the uniformed services are encouraged to render salutes to Medal of Honor recipients as a matter of respect and courtesy, whether or not in uniform and regardless of rank or status.

q: The Enlisted Heritage Hall was developed in which year, and from what original structure?
o: 1983, from a 1942 segregated dining facility
1971, from a 1947 aircraft hangar
1990, from a 1960 barracks
1983, from a 1955 classroom building
why: The 14,000 square foot Enlisted Heritage Hall was developed by the Air Force Senior NCO Academy in 1983 and was originally a 1942 segregated dining facility.

q: The Desert Storm device is awarded for support of operations during which period?
o: 17 January 1991 to 28 February 1991
2 August 1990 to 28 February 1991
11 September 2001 to 31 August 2021
24 March 1999 to 31 December 2013
why: The device is awarded for support of Desert Storm and Liberation of Kuwait in the Persian Gulf, Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Bahrain, Qatar, and UAE, 17 Jan 91 to 28 Feb 91.

q: You are a newly appointed supervisor. A SrA on your team is consistently late and has missed two mandatory training deadlines in the last month. He tells you privately that his spouse is deployed and he is struggling with childcare. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Address the performance directly with him, connect him with Military & Family Readiness and the first sergeant for family support, and document a clear plan with follow-up dates
Say nothing to avoid adding stress and cover his absences yourself
Immediately initiate administrative paperwork to establish a pattern for separation
Announce the issue at the next squadron formation so the team understands the standard
why: Effective supervision corrects the standard while addressing the real cause. AFH 1 emphasizes knowing your Airmen, using support resources (M&FRC, first sergeant, Military & Family Life Counselors), and keeping documentation and follow-up on the standard.

q: During a high-tempo maintenance operation, you notice a troop bypassing a technical order step to save time. He says the expediter told him to 'just get it done.' What is the MOST effective action?
o: Stop the task, apply risk management to the deviation, and notify the expediter and supervisor that TO compliance cannot be bypassed without proper authorization
Let it continue because the expediter has more experience
Document it in the shift log after the task is complete
Ask the troop to sign a statement that he chose to bypass the step
why: Risk management principles apply 24/7 and cannot be overridden by convenience or verbal direction. The correct action halts the unsafe practice, addresses the hazard, and elevates the deviation through the chain.

q: A subordinate tells you in confidence that a coworker made a sexually explicit comment to her. She does not want to make a formal complaint. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Explain her informal and formal options, connect her with the EO office and SARC as appropriate, and take immediate action to address the behavior and prevent reprisal
Promise complete confidentiality and take no further action
Tell her to handle it directly with the coworker as adults
Wait until she decides to file so you avoid overstepping
why: Commanders and supervisors must take immediate and appropriate action once aware of inappropriate behavior or allegations, and are encouraged to consult the EO office before acting. You cannot promise silence that leaves a hostile environment unaddressed.

q: You discover a classified document left on a printer in an unsecured area. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Secure the document immediately, maintain control of it, and report the security incident through the proper channel
Leave it but tell a coworker to watch the area
Photograph it for evidence and return it to the printer for the owner
Discard it in the shred bin and say nothing to avoid getting someone in trouble
why: Each individual is responsible for safeguarding classified information and reporting security incidents. The person with authorized possession must maintain control and keep classified material under constant surveillance.

q: Your flight is tasked with a last-minute mission change. Two Airmen on the team are clearly burned out, and one admits to drinking more on weekends. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Re-brief the task with risk management, redistribute the workload where possible, and connect the Airman with support resources while continuing to monitor
Tell them to push through because the mission comes first
Report the Airman to the commander for an alcohol incident
Ignore the signs until performance degrades
why: Airmen under stress are at elevated risk. AFH 1 calls for recognizing stress, restructuring work where possible, and using support resources — while still accomplishing the mission through sound risk management.

q: A peer NCO asks you to share the questions you remember from last cycle's promotion test to help him study. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Decline, explain that discussing or sharing recalled test content is prohibited under Article 92, and point him to the official study references
Share only the questions you are confident about
Share them but ask him not to tell anyone
Report him to the IG immediately without discussing it
why: Discussing promotion test content with anyone other than the TCO or TE, and sharing recalled questions or personal study materials, is prohibited and punishable under Article 92. The correct action is to refuse, inform, and redirect to official references.

q: You are leading a team and a junior Airman proposes a process change that contradicts how your shop has always done it, but his data suggests it would reduce errors. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Evaluate the data with him, test the change in a controlled way if feasible, and adopt it if it holds up while managing the change with the team
Reject it because he lacks experience and the current process works
Adopt it immediately to encourage initiative
Tell him to submit it through the suggestion program and drop it
why: AFH 1 stresses leaders who are flexible, listen to other points of view, and change course when things are not going well, while the people supporting a change must be motivated to support it.

q: A subordinate's duty performance is strong but his fitness test is overdue and he keeps rescheduling. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Counsel him on the standard and consequences, identify and remove the barrier, and set a firm date with follow-up
Let it go since his work performance is strong
Write him up immediately without a conversation
Report him to the first sergeant and let them handle it
why: Enforcing standards means addressing the deficiency early, understanding the barrier, and following up — not ignoring it because other performance is good, nor escalating before supervising.

q: You are the senior person present when a vehicle mishap injures two Airmen. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Render aid, secure the scene and account for personnel, then report through the chain and preserve information for the investigation
Begin interviewing witnesses to determine fault
Move the vehicle and clean the area before leadership arrives
Wait for security forces before doing anything
why: Immediate priorities are life safety, scene control, accountability, and notification. Determining fault is not the senior present member's role — preserving the scene supports the later investigation (DD Form 200 process for property).

q: A subordinate comes to you saying he is having thoughts of self-harm. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Stay with him, get him to immediate help through the chain and medical or mental health, and ensure he is not left alone
Keep it between the two of you to protect his privacy
Tell him to use the Employee Assistance Program on his own time
Wait to see if he brings it up again
why: The most important step is getting the individual the help they need if in distress. Safety and fitness-for-duty concerns are exactly what providers must disclose to commanders under DoDI 6490.08 — confidentiality does not extend to imminent risk.

q: You are preparing a briefing for the group commander and your facts are incomplete. A peer offers to 'fill in the blanks' with numbers he thinks are close. What is the MOST effective action?
o: State what is verified, clearly identify what is unknown or an estimate, and commit to providing confirmed data by a specific time
Use the peer's numbers since the briefing cannot slip
Omit the section entirely without explanation
Present the estimates as facts to avoid looking unprepared
why: AFH 1 frames the Code of Ethics around integrity and high standards of conduct. Presenting unverified data as fact is misrepresentation; labeling uncertainty and following up protects both the mission and your credibility.

q: Two of your Airmen have an ongoing personal conflict that is starting to affect the shift. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Meet with each individually to understand the issue, set clear behavioral expectations for the workplace, and monitor with follow-up
Order them to stop talking to each other entirely
Counsel both together and warn them of paperwork
Move one to another shift without discussion
why: AFH 1 emphasizes understanding another's position to develop a plan of action that works, appropriate professional relationships, and supervisors addressing inappropriate behavior early.

q: You are assigned a task you have never done before, with a short suspense and no template. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Identify who has done it before, ask for their guidance and any references, then build a draft early enough to get review
Wait for clearer guidance before starting
Build it from scratch without asking anyone so you own it
Delegate it to the most junior Airman on the team
why: Task power and effective development come from knowing who is good at what. Seeking references and early review, rather than guessing or stalling, is how you protect quality against a short suspense.

q: You notice a coworker routinely leaving classified material on his desk overnight in a locked office. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Correct it immediately, remind him of the storage requirement, and report it if it recurs
Ignore it because the office is locked
Report him anonymously without ever speaking to him
Move the material yourself and say nothing
why: Everyone who works with classified information is personally responsible for ensuring unauthorized persons do not gain access, and each individual must report security incidents. Secure it, correct it, and escalate if it repeats.

q: Your team consistently hits its metrics but morale is low and two people have asked for transfers. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Diagnose the cause through candid conversations and feedback, then adjust how work is led — a leader's success is reflected in the followers' morale and enthusiasm
Conclude that the metrics prove leadership is working
Increase production goals to distract from morale
Tell them transfers are a personal decision and take no action
why: AFH 1 states a leader's success is reflected in the efficiency, productivity, morale, and enthusiasm demonstrated by followers. Good metrics alongside attrition and low morale is a leadership signal, not a defense.

q: You are the WAPS monitor's point of contact for your unit. An Airman asks you to hold his highlighted study guide in your office so 'nobody sees him studying.' What is the MOST effective action?
o: Decline the arrangement — highlighted study references may not be shared and study materials cannot be stored or transferred on government systems — and direct him to official electronic references
Hold the materials since you are in a position of trust
Scan and email the guide to your personal account for him
Post the guide on a shared drive so everyone benefits
why: Sharing underlined or highlighted study reference material with other individuals is prohibited, and creating or storing personal study notes on government computers is prohibited. Government computers may only be used to view official electronic references.

q: A senior NCO publicly corrects you in front of your Airmen in a way you believe was unwarranted. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Address it privately with the senior NCO afterward, keep the correction in front of the Airmen professional, and take the substance seriously
Correct him back in front of the Airmen to protect your credibility
Complain to your peers about him
File an IG complaint immediately
why: Maintaining good order and professional relationships means handling the dispute privately while never undermining authority in front of Airmen. Self-aware leaders manage their own reactions rather than projecting them.

q: You are asked to sign for a piece of equipment you have not physically inventoried, and the paperwork is due today. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Inventory the items before signing, document any discrepancies, and inform the accountable property officer
Sign now and inventory later when you have time
Refuse the appointment and walk away from the responsibility
Sign and note 'not verified' in the comments block
why: A property custodian is directly responsible for physical custody, inventory, accounting, and reconciliation. Signing for property you have not verified creates liability under the financial liability investigation process (DD Form 200).

q: Your team is preparing for an inspection and a junior Airman points out that a required record has been missing for months — something a previous supervisor let slide. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Thank him, fix the record now, determine the root cause, and brief your leadership on the gap and the fix
Quietly recreate the record to look current
Blame the previous supervisor in the inspection debrief
Wait to see whether the inspector catches it
why: Integrity requires surfacing and correcting the deficiency rather than fabricating records. Effective leaders treat discovered faults as learning tools and address root cause — falsifying a record is a much larger problem than the original gap.

q: You are mentoring an Airman who wants to make rank but studies only the night before each mock test and scores poorly. What is the MOST effective action?
o: Help him build a self-study plan with short daily sessions and spaced review, and track his progress with him
Tell him to study harder and check back in a month
Give him your notes from last cycle
Advise him that promotion is largely luck and quotas
why: Preparing for promotion testing is an individual responsibility requiring a self-initiated study plan. Spaced, consistent study beats cramming, and a mentor's job is to build the plan and follow up — not to hand over materials that cannot be shared.

q: Which four requirements frame professionalism within the USAF?
o: Trust, loyalty, dignity, and personal commitment
Courage, discipline, teamwork, and readiness
Duty, honor, country, and competence
Integrity, service, excellence, and accountability
why: USAF professionalism is framed by trust, loyalty, dignity, and personal commitment.

q: According to AFH 1, what is at the root of professionalism?
o: Technical competence
Respect
Personal ambition
Strict compliance
why: Respect is the root of professionalism and bonds each Airman's contribution to the mission.

q: Which description best characterizes the USAF as a Total Force?
o: A combat force composed only of Regular Air Force members
A collection of independent components with separate values
A values-based, mission-focused, people-oriented force leveraging officer, enlisted, and civilian Airmen
A joint force administered by the military departments collectively
why: The Total Force leverages officer, enlisted, and civilian Airmen across components and is values-based, mission-focused, and people-oriented.

q: Where should a military professional's primary focus be directed?
o: Promotion and career progression
Pay and future assignments
Personal recognition for mission results
Devoted service to the nation
why: Professional focus must be on devoted service to the nation, not pay or the next assignment.

q: What does AFH 1 identify as the USAF's most important resource?
o: People
Technology
Time
Funding
why: The people-oriented principle states that people are the USAF's most important resource.

q: What distinguishes the profession of arms from other professions?
o: Its members work under civilian supervision
Expertise in the justified application of lethal military force and willingness to make the ultimate sacrifice
Its members must possess a technical specialty
Responsibility for administering national policy
why: The profession is distinguished by expertise in the justified use of lethal military force and members' willingness to make the ultimate sacrifice.

q: What is the result of consistently practicing the virtues associated with the USAF core values?
o: Formal recognition as an ethical leader
Freedom from ethical dilemmas
Habits of honorable thought and action that produce a USAF professional
Uniform decisions across every situation
why: Consistent practice produces habits of honorable thought and action, resulting in a USAF professional.

q: Which set contains the three virtues of Integrity First?
o: Duty, loyalty, and respect
Mission, discipline, and teamwork
Valor, courage, and sacrifice
Honesty, courage, and accountability
why: Honesty, courage, and accountability are the virtues of Integrity First.

q: What does honesty require Airmen to do when evaluating performance?
o: Evaluate against standards and conscientiously and accurately report findings
Report only deficiencies that affect mission completion
Rely on personal judgment instead of published standards
Protect the unit's reputation when deciding what to report
why: Honesty requires evaluation against standards and conscientious, accurate reporting of findings.

q: Which action best demonstrates courage as described in AFH 1?
o: Avoiding risk until fear is eliminated
Admitting a mistake despite possible personal consequences
Following a popular decision without objection
Waiting for others to challenge an improper practice
why: Courage is doing the right thing despite fear and includes taking necessary risks, making unpopular decisions, and admitting mistakes.

q: Which behavior is central to accountability?
o: Delegating responsibility for unfavorable outcomes
Limiting feedback to the formal chain of command
Maintaining transparency, seeking constructive feedback, and owning outcomes
Explaining why circumstances prevented success
why: Accountable individuals remain transparent, seek honest and constructive feedback, and own the outcomes of their actions and decisions.

q: What does Service Before Self require when professional duties conflict with personal desires?
o: Balance both interests equally
Defer the choice to the supervisor
Choose the option with the least personal risk
Give professional duties precedence
why: Service Before Self means professional duties take precedence over personal desires.

q: How does AFH 1 define duty?
o: The obligation to perform what is required for the mission
Voluntary service beyond one's assigned responsibilities
Compliance with a supervisor's personal preferences
The willingness to accept any risk without question
why: Duty is the obligation to perform what is required for the mission.

q: In what order does AFH 1 place an Airman's loyalties?
o: Fellow Airmen, USAF values, then the nation
The nation, USAF values and commitments, then the people with whom one serves
USAF leaders, the unit, then the nation
The mission, personal values, then the chain of command
why: Loyalty is owed first to the nation, second to USAF values and commitments, and finally to fellow service members.

q: How should Airmen most effectively offer alternative solutions and innovative ideas when they disagree with leaders?
o: Through public debate after the decision
By delaying execution until concerns are resolved
Through the chain of command
Only in anonymous feedback
why: AFH 1 directs Airmen to offer alternatives and innovative ideas most effectively through the chain of command.

q: Which three dimensions make up respect?
o: Personal, professional, and institutional respect
Earned, positional, and mutual respect
Individual, team, and mission respect
Self-respect, mutual respect, and organizational respect
why: Respect encompasses self-respect, mutual respect, and organizational respect.

q: What does Excellence In All We Do mean instead of demanding perfection?
o: Continuously advancing the craft and increasing knowledge
Meeting only the minimum standard consistently
Eliminating every possibility of failure
Prioritizing innovation over readiness
why: Excellence means continuously advancing one's craft and knowledge, not demanding perfection from everyone.

q: Which set contains the virtues of Excellence In All We Do?
o: Honesty, courage, and accountability
Mission, discipline, and teamwork
Duty, loyalty, and respect
Innovation, readiness, and resilience
why: Mission, discipline, and teamwork are the virtues of Excellence In All We Do.

q: Which action reflects teamwork as described in AFH 1?
o: Focusing only on one's assigned share of the mission
Waiting for leaders to resolve a teammate's workload problem
Carrying one's own weight and helping wingmen carry theirs when necessary
Competing with peers to establish individual credibility
why: Teamwork requires giving one's best, carrying one's weight, and helping wingmen when necessary.

q: Why is merely following the law insufficient under the USAF code of ethics?
o: Laws apply only to conduct performed on duty
Commanders may disregard laws for mission needs
Ethics replaces legal requirements in military service
Law states what can or cannot be done, while ethics addresses what should or should not be done
why: Law defines what is permitted or prohibited; ethics provides the broader standard of what one should or should not do.

q: Which action is consistent with the ethical rules governing federal property?
o: Protecting and conserving federal property and using it only for authorized activities
Using federal property for personal purposes when no cost is incurred
Allowing a non-Federal organization preferential access for a worthy cause
Making an unofficial promise that commits government resources
why: Employees must protect and conserve federal property and use it only for authorized activities.

q: Which morality test asks how a decision would look if aired on the news or social media?
o: The Divine Test
The Network Test
The United States of America Test
The Public Trust Test
why: The Network Test asks whether one would be proud or ashamed if the action were broadcast publicly.

q: Which sequence correctly reflects the priorities examined by the United States of America Test?
o: Self, unit, USAF, United States
Unit, self, USAF, United States
United States, USAF, unit, self
USAF, United States, self, unit
why: The test asks in order whether the decision is good for the United States, the USAF, the unit, and oneself.

q: Which type of courage is the ability to stand by the core values when doing so may be unpopular?
o: Personal courage
Physical courage
Professional courage
Moral courage
why: Moral courage is standing by the core values even when that position may be unpopular.

q: How does AFH 1 define valor?
o: The ability to face danger or hardship in a determined and resolute manner
The absence of fear during combat
The willingness to sacrifice only in wartime
The authority to accept risk on behalf of others
why: Valor is the ability to face danger or hardship with determination and resolve.

q: What is command authority?
o: The personal influence a commander exercises over assigned members
Established levels of responsibility for command, control, and communication throughout a chain of command
The authority military departments retain over combatant operations
The statutory power of the Joint Chiefs to command forces
why: Command authority consists of established responsibility levels for command, control, and communication throughout the chain.

q: For forces assigned to combatant commanders, what typically remains with the respective service branch?
o: Operational control
Combatant command authority
Administrative control
Authority to transfer the force
why: Although assigned forces fall under the combatant command chain, administrative control typically flows through the service branch.

q: What is the Department of Defense mission?
o: Develop joint doctrine and coordinate military education
Formulate national policy and supervise Congress
Provide homeland civil support to state governments
Provide military forces to deter war and protect the security of the country
why: The Department of Defense provides military forces to deter war and protect national security.

q: Who serves as the U.S. President's principal defense policy advisor?
o: The Secretary of Defense
The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
The National Security Advisor
The Secretary of the Air Force
why: The Secretary of Defense is the President's principal defense policy advisor.

q: By law, who has exclusive direction of the Joint Staff?
o: The Secretary of Defense
The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
The Director of the Joint Staff
The Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
why: Direction of the Joint Staff rests exclusively with the Chairman, who normally manages it through the Director.

ref: AFH 1, 5.3, Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff
q: Which statement correctly describes the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff's command authority?
o: The Chairman commands all combatant commanders
The Chairman commands the Joint Chiefs but not service forces
The Chairman outranks all other officers but may not exercise military command over the Joint Chiefs or Armed Forces
The Chairman commands forces only when acting for the Secretary of Defense
why: Although the senior-ranking officer, the Chairman may not exercise military command over the Joint Chiefs or Armed Forces.

ref: AFH 1, 5.3, Vice Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff
q: Which restriction applies to the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff?
o: The Vice Chairman may serve only one two-year term
The Vice Chairman must be from the same service as the Chairman
The Vice Chairman cannot act for the Chairman
The Vice Chairman cannot be from the same service branch as the Chairman
why: The Vice Chairman cannot be from the Chairman's branch and serves as Acting Chairman when required.

ref: AFH 1, 5.3, Senior Enlisted Advisor to the Chairman
q: What is the Senior Enlisted Advisor to the Chairman designated as?
o: The highest senior enlisted position in the U.S. Armed Forces
The senior enlisted commander of all joint forces
The enlisted member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
The Department of Defense career field manager
why: The SEAC is designated as the highest senior enlisted position in the U.S. Armed Forces.

q: What agreement established the general and specific functions of each branch of the U.S. Armed Forces?
o: The Unified Command Plan
The Key West Agreement of 1948
The Goldwater-Nichols Act
The National Security Act of 1947
why: The Secretary of Defense and Joint Chiefs established service roles and missions in the 1948 Key West Agreement.

ref: AFH 1, 5.5, Functions of the United States Coast Guard
q: When does the Coast Guard operate as part of the Navy rather than as a Department of Homeland Security service?
o: Whenever it performs maritime law enforcement
Whenever it operates outside U.S. waters
Upon a declaration of war or when directed by the President
Only during a national emergency declared by Congress
why: The Coast Guard is in the Department of Homeland Security except when operating as part of the Navy upon declaration of war or presidential direction.

ref: AFH 1, 5.5, Functions of the United States Space Force
q: Which is a specific Space Force function listed in AFH 1?
o: Control all military cyberspace operations
Provide strategic airlift to joint forces
Administer civilian space agencies
Provide freedom of operation for the United States in, from, and to space
why: A stated Space Force function is providing U.S. freedom of operation in, from, and to space.

q: What makes a command a combined command?
o: It includes two or more forces or agencies from two or more allied nations operating together
It includes forces from two or more U.S. military departments
It combines operational and administrative control
It operates across more than one geographic region
why: Combined commands consist of forces or agencies of at least two allies operating together under multinational arrangements.

q: Which feature defines a unified combatant command?
o: A temporary mission limited to one military department
A broad, continuing mission composed of forces from two or more military departments
A multinational mission established only by treaty
A global functional mission with no assigned forces
why: A unified combatant command has a broad, continuing mission and forces from two or more military departments.

q: How often is the Unified Command Plan reviewed and updated?
o: Annually
Every four years
Every two years
Only when combatant command boundaries change
why: The classified Unified Command Plan is reviewed and updated every two years.

q: How do functional combatant commands differ from geographic combatant commands?
o: They exercise administrative control instead of operational authority
They consist of only one military department
They are temporary commands activated for contingencies
They operate globally across geographic boundaries based on military function
why: Functional combatant commands operate globally across geographic boundaries and provide unique capabilities.

q: What are U.S. Northern Command's primary responsibilities?
o: Civil support and homeland security
Strategic deterrence and global strike
Special operations and counterterrorism
Global mobility and distribution
why: USNORTHCOM is primarily responsible for civil support and homeland security.

q: What is U.S. Cyber Command responsible for achieving and maintaining?
o: Information dominance
Cyberspace superiority
Electromagnetic spectrum control
Global communications readiness
why: USCYBERCOM is responsible for achieving and maintaining cyberspace superiority.

q: In a classic Total Force association, which organization is the host and retains weapon-system responsibility?
o: The Reserve unit
The Guard unit
The Regular Component
The combatant command
why: In a classic association, the Regular Component hosts and retains weapon-system responsibility while sharing the mission.

q: In an active Total Force association, which unit serves as the host?
o: The Regular Component unit
The MAJCOM headquarters
The active-duty service component
The Reserve or Guard unit
why: In an active association, the Reserve or Guard unit hosts and the Regular Component is the tenant.

q: Which two components form the Air Reserve Component?
o: The Air National Guard and USAF Reserve
The USAF Reserve and Civil Air Patrol
The Air National Guard and Regular Air Force
The Civil Air Patrol and Air National Guard
why: The Air National Guard and USAF Reserve together form the Air Reserve Component.

ref: AFH 1, 5.11, Dual Federal and State Mission
q: Who has command jurisdiction over an Air National Guard unit when it is not mobilized or under federal control?
o: The Secretary of the Air Force
The governor of the state, commonwealth, or possession
The Chief of the National Guard Bureau

q: When does DoD begin the automatic one-percent base-pay contribution for a member enrolled in BRS?
o: After 60 days of service
Immediately upon accession
After two years of service
After completion of the first enlistment
why: The automatic one-percent contribution begins after 60 days; matching contributions begin after two years.

q: What percentage of applicable retired pay does the Survivor Benefit Plan annuity provide in the death cases described in AFH 1?
o: 50 percent
55 percent
60 percent
75 percent
why: The described annuity is 55 percent of the retired pay the member would have been entitled to receive under the applicable calculation.

q: When does the Survivor Benefit Plan's paid-up feature allow a participant to stop paying premiums while retaining coverage?
o: At age 65 after 240 monthly premiums
At age 70 regardless of payment history
At age 70 after paying premiums for 360 months
After 30 years of military service
why: Paid-up status requires both attainment of age 70 and payment of SBP premiums for 360 months.

q: What status may the WEAR program grant for participation in an event that directly enhances recruiting?
o: Non-chargeable leave
Funded temporary duty
A four-day special pass
Permissive temporary duty
why: WEAR may authorize permissive TDY for approved events that directly support the recruiting mission.

q: For leave purposes, what is the member's local area?
o: The place of residence from which the member commutes daily to the duty station
Any location within the state of assignment
Any location within one day's driving distance
The area inside the installation's official boundaries
why: Leave must begin and end in the local area, defined as the residence from which the member normally commutes to duty.

q: How much leave does a member accrue for each month of RegAF status?
o: Two days
Two and one-half days
Three days
Three and one-half days
why: Members accrue 2.5 days of leave for each month in RegAF status.

q: Which statement correctly describes emergency leave?
o: It is always non-chargeable and limited to 14 days
It is ordinary leave available only for a member's own illness
It is chargeable leave for immediate-family emergencies, usually initially limited to 30 days
It is permissive TDY approved only by the installation commander
why: Emergency leave is chargeable, concerns immediate-family emergencies, and normally begins with no more than 30 days.

q: How often may Emergency Leave of Absence be granted during a service member's career?
o: Once per enlistment
Once per qualifying family member
Once every five years
Once during the entire career
why: This non-chargeable absence of up to 14 days may be used once in an entire career to prevent advance or excess leave.

q: How much non-chargeable leave does the Military Parental Leave Program authorize after a qualifying event?
o: 12 weeks
6 weeks
14 days
30 days
why: Covered service members receive 12 weeks after a qualifying birth, adoption, or placement for adoption or long-term foster care.

q: Which rule applies to permissive temporary duty?
o: It may replace annual leave when a member lacks a leave balance
It may not be authorized in place of leave or a special pass, or in conjunction with special passes
It must always involve travel outside the local area
It is limited to house-hunting near a new duty station
why: Permissive TDY is an administrative absence and cannot substitute for leave or a special pass or be combined with special passes.

q: What are the three primary sources of civilian employee training?
o: On-the-job, classroom, and distance learning
Local, major-command, and Headquarters Air Force
Agency, interagency, and nongovernment
Mandatory, voluntary, and developmental
why: AFH 1 groups civilian training sources as agency, interagency, and nongovernment.

q: What are the normal annual-leave accumulation caps for most civilian employees and for employees working overseas?
o: 20 days and 30 days, respectively
30 days for both groups
45 days and 60 days, respectively
30 days and 45 days, respectively
why: Most civilian employees may accumulate 30 days of annual leave; employees overseas may accumulate 45 days.

q: What does a member's military pay date determine?
o: Length of service for pay purposes
Date of eligibility for retirement
Date annual leave begins to accrue
Length of service for promotion testing
why: The military pay date determines length of service for pay purposes and may be adjusted for creditable prior service or certain absences.

q: After an electronic funds transfer, how is a partial pay payment normally recovered?
o: In equal installments over the next 12 months
In full on the next available payday
Only after the member submits a repayment agreement
From the member's next travel settlement
why: Partial payments are limited to accrued pay and allowances and are recouped in full on the next available payday.

q: Which statement correctly describes overseas housing allowance?
o: It is a flat taxable payment unrelated to actual rent
It is paid only during temporary duty outside the United States
It reimburses actual rent up to the locality, grade, and dependency-status maximum
It replaces all utility and maintenance reimbursements with basic allowance for housing
why: Overseas housing allowance is cost-reimbursement based; actual rent is reimbursed up to the applicable maximum, with a utility/recurring-maintenance allowance included monthly.

q: When does the standard clothing replacement allowance normally replace the basic clothing replacement allowance?
o: After 12 months of RegAF status
Upon promotion to staff sergeant
At the member's first permanent change of station
After 36 months of RegAF status
why: The basic allowance is paid annually between months 6 and 36 of RegAF status; the standard allowance automatically replaces it after 36 months.

q: When can family separation allowance-temporary apply?
o: When a member is continuously TDY away from the permanent duty station for more than 30 days and dependents are not at or near the TDY location
Whenever dependents remain behind during any TDY of at least 14 days
Only when dependent transportation is prohibited during a PCS
Whenever a member occupies government quarters without dependents
why: Family separation allowance-temporary applies to continuous TDY exceeding 30 days when dependents do not reside at or near the TDY station.

q: Which member may qualify for the Basic Needs Allowance described in AFH 1?
o: Any member whose basic pay is below the national median income
An Airman or Guardian who voluntarily applies and whose gross household income and household size fall below 150 percent of the applicable federal poverty guideline
Only an enlisted member assigned to government quarters with dependents
Any member receiving food assistance from a state program
why: The taxable monthly Basic Needs Allowance is for Airmen and Guardians who voluntarily apply and fall below 150 percent of the federal poverty guideline for their household size and location.

q: How are Traditional and Roth TSP contributions treated for income-tax purposes?
o: Both are contributed after taxes and withdrawn tax-free
Both reduce current taxable income and are taxed at withdrawal
Traditional contributions may be made before taxes, while Roth contributions are made after taxes and their contributions are tax-free when withdrawn
Traditional contributions are tax-free only for deployed members, while Roth contributions are always taxable at withdrawal
why: Traditional TSP contributions can reduce current taxable income; Roth contributions are taxed before contribution, so those contributions are tax-free upon withdrawal.

q: Who rules on all requests to waive U.S. claims for erroneous payments of pay and allowances?
o: The member's immediate commander
The local financial services office
The Secretary of the Air Force
The Defense Finance and Accounting Service
why: A waiver may be available absent fraud, misrepresentation, fault, or lack of good faith, but DFAS rules on all waivers.

q: Which PCS advance-pay request requires the Airman's immediate commander's approval?
