o: A request by an E-3 or below, a request for more than one month's basic pay, or a repayment period longer than 12 months
Every PCS advance-pay request, regardless of grade or amount
Only a request exceeding three months of basic pay
Only a request from an Airman without dependents
why: Commander approval is required for E-3 and below and for any request exceeding one month's basic pay or a 12-month repayment period.

q: What is the maximum net weight of unaccompanied baggage that may be moved by commercial air as an expedited PCS shipment?
o: 500 pounds
1,000 pounds
1,500 pounds
2,000 pounds
why: When commercial air is used as the expedited mode, no more than 1,000 pounds net of unaccompanied baggage may be transported.

q: How do temporary lodging expense and temporary lodging allowance differ during a PCS?
o: Both apply only outside CONUS, but one covers meals and the other lodging
Temporary lodging expense is paid through military pay, while temporary lodging allowance is paid on a travel voucher
Temporary lodging expense applies within CONUS and is paid on a travel voucher; temporary lodging allowance applies outside CONUS and appears in military pay
Temporary lodging expense is for members with dependents, while temporary lodging allowance is for members without dependents
why: TLE helps with temporary lodging during a CONUS PCS and is voucher-paid; TLA applies outside CONUS and is paid through military pay and shown on the LES.

q: A traveler returns from official travel. By when should the traveler file the DTS voucher or DD Form 1351-2?
o: Within 24 hours
Within three calendar days
Within ten business days
Within five business days after returning to the permanent duty station
why: Travelers are responsible for filing electronically in DTS or preparing DD Form 1351-2 within five business days after return to their permanent duty station.

q: What voucher arrangement is required in DTS for a TDY lasting 45 days or more?
o: An interim voucher or scheduled partial payments every 30 days, using split disbursement
One final voucher filed within 45 days of return
Weekly vouchers paid entirely to the traveler
A cash advance in place of all vouchers
why: For TDY of 45 days or more, DTS must establish an interim voucher or scheduled partial payments every 30 days and use split disbursement for timely GTCC payment.

q: How early may a traveler normally obtain a GTCC automated teller machine advance?
o: No earlier than seven calendar days before travel
No earlier than three working days before scheduled travel
Only after arriving at the TDY location
At any time after travel orders are published
why: GTCC ATM advances may not be obtained earlier than three working days before scheduled travel and are limited to authorized expenses exempt from mandatory card use.

q: What happens when a GTCC account reaches 31 days past due?
o: DFAS immediately begins salary offset
The account is permanently charged off
The account is suspended, and the cardholder must contact the agency program coordinator
The vendor automatically places the member on a reduced payment plan
why: At 31 days past due the account is suspended, and the cardholder must work with the APC to resolve the delinquency.

q: Which three types of manpower are used to conduct the USAF mission?
o: Active duty, Air Force Reserve, and Air National Guard
Officers, enlisted members, and civilians
Permanent, temporary, and seasonal personnel
Military personnel, in-service civilian employees, and contracted services
why: AFH 1 identifies military personnel, in-service civilian employees, and contracted services as the three manpower types used for the USAF mission.

q: What is the Unit Manpower Document?
o: The primary, computer-generated document listing a unit's funded and unfunded manpower requirements
A quarterly roster of personnel actually assigned to a unit
A budget document listing only civilian authorizations
A deployment document identifying wartime taskings
why: The UMD is the primary document reflecting manpower required for the unit mission and lists both funded and unfunded requirements.

q: Which function is excluded from Commercial Services Management actions?
o: A function currently performed by contractors
A military-essential skill or inherently governmental function
A function that could be evaluated through competitive sourcing
A support activity with measurable costs
why: Commercial Services Management will not affect military-essential skills or functions that are inherently governmental.

q: What does a competitive sourcing study compare?
o: Two private contractors' technical proposals only
Military and civilian promotion systems
The total cost of an in-house government operation with the total cost of private-sector performance of the same activity
Current mission output with the prior year's output
why: Competitive sourcing is a public-private competition that determines whether government or private-sector performance is the more economical or efficient approach.

q: Who appoints a resource advisor in writing?
o: The installation commander
The comptroller
The financial management board
The responsibility center manager
why: Resource advisors are appointed in writing by the responsibility center manager and serve as the primary resource-management contact for that responsibility center.

q: What is the relationship between the Financial Working Group and the Financial Management Board?
o: The working group develops financial-plan requirements and recommendations; the board reviews them and gives final approval or disapproval
The board prepares cost-center estimates; the working group audits them
The working group allocates funds without board review
The board handles only nonappropriated funds, while the working group handles appropriated funds
why: The FWG develops and revises plans and recommends priorities or target adjustments; the FMB reviews those recommendations and approves or disapproves them.

q: During which PPBE phase does the USAF match fiscal, manpower, and materiel resources against validated requirements to develop the Program Objective Memorandum?
o: Planning
Programming
Budgeting
Execution
why: Programming matches available resources to validated requirements, with the key objective of developing a balanced, capabilities-based Air Force POM.

q: When is the Future Years Defense Program normally updated during a PPBE cycle?
o: Monthly throughout execution
Only when Congress passes an appropriation
At POM submission, usually July or August, and again at the President's budget submission in early February
At the start and end of every fiscal quarter
why: The FYDP is updated twice: upon POM submission, normally July/August, and upon the President's budget submission in early February of the following year.

q: Which description best distinguishes waste from fraud?
o: Waste requires theft, while fraud does not
Waste is always prosecutable, while fraud is only administrative
Waste is any intentional misuse of rank, while fraud is an accounting error
Waste is extravagant, careless, or needless expenditure arising from deficient practices or decisions; fraud involves intentional deception or diversion for an unauthorized benefit
why: Waste may result from deficient practices and need not involve prosecutable fraud; fraud requires intentional deception or diversion to deprive the USAF or secure an unauthorized benefit.

q: What is the correct sequence of the four Environmental Management System phases?
o: Plan, Do, Check, Act
Assess, Plan, Execute, Review
Identify, Reduce, Monitor, Report
Plan, Fund, Implement, Audit
why: The four EMS phases are Plan, Do, Check, and Act; they move from defining scope and objectives through implementation, monitoring, and management review.

q: What does AFH 1 identify as the core of all healthy team interaction?
o: Competition
Trust
Technical expertise
Formal authority
why: Healthy teams rest on trust, communication, and cooperation, with trust at the core of healthy team interaction.

q: A team is cautiously testing acceptable behavior and transitioning from individual to member status. Which stage is it experiencing?
o: Storming
Norming
Forming
Performing
why: Forming is the initial period of uncertainty when members explore boundaries, determine their places, and accept team procedures and rules.

q: During which team-development stage do members reconcile competing loyalties, accept team roles and norms, and become more cooperative?
o: Forming
Storming
Performing
Norming
why: During norming, members establish cohesion, accept the team and its rules and roles, and shift from competitive to cooperative relationships.

q: When does conflict become destructive?
o: When it creates barriers to cooperation and communication, degrades morale, and diverts attention from tasks
Whenever two members openly disagree
When it produces several possible alternatives
Whenever a leader becomes involved in resolving it
why: Conflict is destructive when it obstructs cooperation and communication, lowers morale, and pulls attention away from the work.

q: Which is a structural factor that can generate organizational conflict?
o: A member's personal values
Scarce or heavily demanded resources
An individual's personality
A misunderstood message
why: Structural sources include organizational size, resource scarcity or high demand, interaction among more people, and line-staff distinctions.

q: Which conflict-management style combines high assertiveness with high cooperativeness and seeks a win for both sides?
o: Competing
Accommodating
Collaborating
Avoiding
why: Collaborating uses honest discussion to satisfy both sides and requires trust and openness from all participants.

q: Which conflict-management style uses some assertiveness and some cooperativeness, with both parties giving something up?
o: Competing
Avoiding
Accommodating
Compromising
why: Compromising partially satisfies both parties and requires each to change, adjust, or surrender something.

q: Which three behavioral characteristics did Warren Bennis associate with managers?
o: Administrators, maintainers, and controllers
Motivators, developers, and inspirers
Planners, organizers, and mentors
Innovators, collaborators, and coaches
why: Bennis characterized managers as administrators, maintainers, and controllers; he associated motivating, developing, and inspiring with leaders.

q: At a minimum, what must a supervisor's mentoring include?
o: A quarterly written career-development plan
Discussion of performance, potential, and professional-development plans during performance feedback sessions
Assignment of a mentor outside the chain of command
Annual review by the command chief
why: The minimum mentoring obligation is a performance-feedback discussion covering performance, potential, and professional-development plans.

q: Who is the primary mentor, coach, counselor, guide, or role model under the Air Force Mentoring Program?
o: The first sergeant
The command chief
The immediate supervisor or rater
The career field manager
why: The immediate supervisor or rater is the primary mentor, although Airmen may seek advice from additional mentors.

q: In the M-E-N-T-O-R-I-N-G model, which element requires active listening, attention to nonverbal cues, and timely answers?
o: Empathize
Teach
Network
Respond
why: Respond treats mentoring as two-way communication and calls for active listening, recognition of subtle cues, anticipation of needs, and useful timely responses.

q: What does the Network element of effective mentoring require?
o: Connecting the protégé with people who can provide guidance, support, resources, and opportunities
Teaching the protégé to use official computer networks
Assigning the protégé to a different organization
Limiting advice to the mentor's own expertise
why: A good mentor helps the protégé establish a professional network by making connections to additional sources of guidance and opportunity.

q: When should counseling normally be conducted for the best chance of success?
o: At the end of the rating period
As close to the event as possible
Only after a pattern of behavior is established
At the next scheduled performance feedback session
why: AFH 1 states that the key to successful counseling is conducting it as close to the event as possible.

q: Which counseling approach is preferred for most sessions and has the leader help the Airman explore the situation without supplying the solution?
o: Directive
Combined
Nondirective
Referral
why: Nondirective counseling emphasizes listening and helping the Airman clarify and decide while the leader refrains from giving solutions or opinions.

q: When is directive counseling most appropriate?
o: When the Airman should independently discover a solution
When the issue is emotionally complex and time is plentiful
When several equally good solutions require group analysis
When time is short, the solution is clear, or the Airman needs guidance because of limited problem-solving skill
why: Directive counseling works best for simple problems, on-the-spot corrections, and specific performance issues when time is short or clear guidance is needed.

q: What are the four basic components of a counseling session, in order?
o: State the purpose, discuss the issues, develop a plan of action, and record the plan
Gather evidence, state the standard, issue a decision, and notify the chain
Establish rapport, identify blame, impose consequences, and schedule review
Define the problem, select an approach, refer the Airman, and close the session
why: Even without formal preparation, a leader can follow the sequence: state purpose, discuss issues, develop the action plan, and record it.

q: How should leaders treat an organizational vision as conditions change?
o: Replace it on a fixed annual schedule
Continually reassess it, revising when needed but affirming it when it remains effective and aligned
Preserve it unchanged to demonstrate consistency
Allow only senior leadership to communicate or evaluate it
why: Vision formation should be continual, but a working vision aligned with environmental and technological developments should not be arbitrarily changed.

q: How should responsibility increase when developing Airmen for leadership positions?
o: Only after the Airman has mastered every current duty
In a single major step to test potential
Gradually, through consistent exposure to challenges over time
Only when a formal leadership billet becomes vacant
why: Developing leaders requires consistent challenge with gradual increases in responsibility, matched to each Airman's capabilities.

q: Which source of power comes from association with others through friendship, familiarity, cultivated relationships, or reciprocity?
o: Position power
Knowledge power
Personal power
Relationship power
why: Relationship power derives from connections and reciprocity, though perceived favoritism can harm an organization.

q: What three core elements make up Full Range Leadership Development as a system?
o: The leader, the follower, and the situation
The mission, the organization, and the environment
Authority, responsibility, and accountability
Vision, communication, and motivation
why: FRLD requires attention not only to the leader's actions but also to the follower and the situation.

q: Which leadership behavior waits for policies, rules, or goals to be violated before intervening?
o: Laissez-faire
Management by exception-passive
Management by exception-active
Contingent reward
why: Management by exception-passive follows an 'if it is not broken, do not fix it' approach and acts only after standards are missed or rules are broken.

q: In Full Range Leadership Development, what makes a reward 'contingent'?
o: The reward depends on available unit funds
The follower chooses the reward before accepting the task
The leader provides it after the follower performs assigned tasks to the specified expectation
The commander approves it only after an annual review
why: Contingent reward is a constructive transaction: the leader sets and supports the goal, and reinforcement follows performance to the agreed standard.

q: Which transformational component seeks different perspectives, considers opposing views, and encourages independent thought and creativity?
o: Individualized consideration
Idealized influence
Inspirational motivation
Intellectual stimulation
why: Intellectual stimulation values followers' rationality, solicits different views and ideas, and encourages creativity and independent thinking.

q: What is the first step in leading a diverse organization?
o: Establish common ground through shared assumptions such as the organization's vision, goals, rules, and processes
Assign members to groups based on similar backgrounds
Eliminate all differences in individual work methods
Begin with a formal assessment of every member's cultural identity
why: Common ground creates the framework for communication and direction through the organization's shared vision, goals, rules, regulations, processes, and procedures.

q: What are the three commitment levels in contemporary motivation, from lowest to highest?
o: Compliance, contribution, commitment
Membership, performance, involvement
Awareness, acceptance, advocacy
Participation, proficiency, ownership
why: The model progresses from membership at the lowest level, through performance, to involvement at the highest level.

q: How does AFH 1 define self-efficacy?
o: Freedom to act without supervision
The ability to suppress emotional reactions
A person's belief in the ability to address a situation based on available skills and circumstances
A willingness to accept responsibility for a team's failures
why: Self-efficacy is confidence in one's ability to address a situation based on personal skills and the circumstances faced.

q: In the context of personal responsibility, what does autonomy mean?
o: Following the choice preferred by the group
Acting only within one's technical specialty
Avoiding action until formal authority is granted
Recognizing that you choose your own actions or inactions and can support the greater good despite pressure
why: Autonomy means exercising personal control over one's response rather than surrendering that choice to pressure from leaders or friends.

q: Which belief reflects a growth mindset?
o: Past mistakes do not define a person's capacity to improve and change
Effort demonstrates a lack of natural ability
Intelligence and personal qualities are mostly permanent
Early failure reliably predicts future limits
why: A growth mindset recognizes the capacity for fundamental improvement and does not treat past failure as a permanent definition of ability.

q: How do people with a growth mindset typically respond to criticism and others' success?
o: They avoid both to protect confidence
They seek feedback, learn from criticism, and find lessons or inspiration in others' success
They treat criticism as proof of fixed limitations
They compete to demonstrate superior natural talent
why: Growth-minded people use feedback and criticism to improve and do not feel threatened by others' achievements.

q: Why does AFH 1 recommend changing a situation to reduce temptation rather than relying only on willpower?
o: Temptation cannot be resisted under any circumstances
Environmental changes permanently eliminate impulses
Self-control is limited and can be depleted by heavy use
Willpower works only for physical habits, not emotions
why: Because self-control is finite, removing triggers or temptations often prevents inappropriate behavior more reliably than repeatedly exerting internal restraint.

q: Which practice does AFH 1 identify as a way to strengthen self-control?
o: Attempting one exhausting act of restraint each month
Avoiding every situation requiring restraint
Practicing only in the area where self-control is weakest
Regularly practicing small acts of restraint with rest and recording the effort
why: Small, deliberate acts of self-control, interspersed with rest and tracked through daily records, can strengthen impulse control over time.

q: What is positive reappraisal?
o: Reinterpreting stressful events as nonthreatening, meaningful, or capable of contributing to growth
Denying that a negative event occurred
Replacing a difficult task with an easier one
Evaluating another person's performance positively
why: Positive reappraisal actively finds meaning and growth in adversity; it is not wishful denial of reality.

q: Compared with framing a stressful event as a threat, what tends to happen when it is framed as a challenge?
o: The person reports more anxiety but performs faster
The person reports less anxiety and physiological measures return to normal more quickly
The person's heart rate remains elevated longer
The person no longer needs preparation or practice
why: Challenge framing is associated with less anxiety and faster recovery of heart rate, pulse, and blood pressure after the event.

q: How is strategic communication implemented in practical terms?
o: By separating public messages from operational actions
By maximizing the number of messages sent to an audience
By aligning actions, words, and images to obtain a specific objective
By delegating all external communication to Public Affairs
why: Strategic communication synchronizes information and other elements of power by aligning what an organization does, says, and shows with its objectives.

q: What role does the Public Affairs representative hold for a commander?
o: Records manager and security reviewer
Primary liaison to the inspector general
Advisor only for domestic media interviews
Principal spokesperson and advisor, serving as a member of the personal staff
why: PA is the commander's principal spokesperson and advisor and advises on how decisions, actions, and operations affect domestic and foreign perceptions.

q: Which information may not be posted to social networking services or sent through non-DoD e-mail without proper authority?
o: Classified information, controlled unclassified information, and other official DoD information and documents
Only information marked Top Secret
Any personal opinion about military service
Publicly released news from official websites
why: Operations security rules prohibit posting classified, controlled unclassified, and other official DoD information or documents without proper authority.

q: Which five qualities must an effective organizational culture possess?
o: Accurate, brief, clear, timely, and secure
Proactive, innovative, adaptive, leader driven, and sustainable
Formal, centralized, standardized, measured, and controlled
Focused, organized, clear, understanding, and supported
why: AFH 1 identifies proactive, innovative, adaptive, leader-driven, and sustainable as the qualities of an effective culture of engagement.

q: Which set correctly expands the FOCUS principles of effective communication?
o: Formal, objective, concise, useful, secure
Focused, ordered, credible, unified, specific
Focused, organized, clear, understanding, supported
Facts, options, conclusions, urgency, suspense
why: FOCUS stands for focused, organized, clear, understanding, and supported.

q: Which sequence correctly gives the seven steps for effective communication?
o: Research, analyze, outline, support, draft, approve, edit
Analyze, support, research, draft, organize, edit, approve
Analyze, research, draft, organize, support, edit, approve
Analyze purpose and audience; research; support ideas; organize and outline; draft; edit; fight for feedback and get approval
why: The first four steps lay groundwork, followed by drafting, editing, and actively seeking feedback and approval.

q: During the edit step, in what order should a communicator review a draft?
o: Big picture and flow; paragraph structure and support; then sentences, words, and grammar
Grammar first; citations second; purpose and organization last
Format first; audience second; supporting evidence last
Word choice first; paragraph order second; topic selection last
why: Editing proceeds from the overall purpose, length, and flow, to paragraphs and support, and finally to sentence-level wording and mechanics.

q: When is a face-to-face meeting generally more appropriate than e-mail or a phone call?
o: When a short message needs no response
When multiple people must engage in dialogue, possibly on a recurring basis
When the sender wants to avoid cross-talk
When information must be delivered without clarification
why: Meetings are suited to multi-person dialogue for sharing information, solving problems, planning, brainstorming, motivating, or making decisions.

q: Which guidance applies to a personal letter?
o: Use it for routine official coordination between federal offices
Use acronyms to keep the letter within one page
Use it when warmth or sincerity is desired, keep it preferably to one page, and avoid acronyms
Use it only for correspondence with vendors and contractors
why: A personal letter suits private matters such as praise, condolence, or sponsorship and should be brief and free of acronyms.

q: Which paper is a single-page memory jogger using minimal bullets or phrases for a single issue, often with little or no notice?
o: Talking paper
Background paper
Position paper
Point paper
why: The point paper is a one-page, minimal-text outline used to quickly inform or cue a speaker, including in extemporaneous situations.

q: What is the purpose of a staff study?
o: To analyze a problem, draw conclusions, and make recommendations
To provide a one-page chronology in bullet format
To advocate a proposal without presenting analysis
To serve as the cover page for routed correspondence
why: A staff study is a multi-page research paper that uses detailed discussion, conclusions, and recommendations as a written problem-solving process.

q: What is the AF Form 1768, Staff Summary Sheet, within a staff package?
o: The final approval memorandum
The first-page cover that condenses the package's purpose, background, discussion, views, recommendation, signatures, and contents
A routing log used only for classified correspondence
An attachment listing all source citations
why: The SSS, Triple-S, or e-SSS is the cover page and condensed summary of a staff package.

q: Which delivery format uses a thoroughly planned and practiced outline while allowing the actual words to sound spontaneous and natural?
o: Impromptu
Manuscript
Prepared
Formal lecture
why: Prepared delivery uses careful planning, practice, and a thorough outline rather than a memorized script, so the wording remains natural.

q: Which quality most clearly distinguishes a briefing from other types of speaking?
o: Accuracy
Clarity
Audience interaction
Brevity
why: Accuracy and clarity characterize good speaking generally, but brevity distinguishes a briefing.

q: What should a briefer do when unable to answer an audience question?
o: Request time to research it and provide a later follow-up rather than improvise an answer
Offer the most likely answer and label it as an estimate
Redirect the question to another audience member
Omit the question from the record and continue
why: AFH 1 directs briefers not to answer off the cuff when they do not know; they should research and follow up.

q: Why should writers be especially careful with humor, irony, and sarcasm in e-mail?
o: They are prohibited in every government message
Without body language, vocal tone, and other nonverbal cues, recipients may perceive them more harshly than intended
They prevent digital signatures from validating
They automatically make the message an official record
why: E-mail removes nonverbal context, so intended humor or sarcasm is easily misread and may appear harsher than the sender intended.

q: What should a user do upon noticing antivirus errors, virus alerts, unexpected file-size increases, unexpected disk access, or strange application behavior?
o: Restart the system and report only if the issue returns
Delete the affected files before notifying anyone
Report the suspected information-system abnormality immediately to the organizational information assurance officer
Disconnect the system and attempt to remove the malware personally
why: Suspected malicious-logic symptoms must be reported immediately to the organizational information assurance officer.

q: Which sequence states the five mission areas in the DAF Emergency Management Program's primary mission?
o: Detect, deter, defend, defeat, and recover
Prevent, protect, prepare for, respond to, and recover from hazards and threats
Plan, organize, equip, train, and evaluate
Warn, shelter, evacuate, account for, and restore
why: The primary mission is to prevent, protect, prepare for, respond to, and recover from hazards and threats posing the greatest risk.

q: In emergency management, which mission area consists of actions to avoid an incident or intervene to stop it from occurring?
o: Recovery
Mitigation
Prevention
Response
why: Prevention consists of actions that avoid an incident or intervene to stop one from occurring.

q: Which emergency management mission area addresses the short-term, direct effects of an incident and includes immediate life-saving actions?
o: Protection
Recovery
Prevention
Response
why: Response addresses short-term direct effects and includes immediate actions to save lives, protect property, and meet basic human needs.

q: Emergency management measures that reduce or eliminate risk and may occur before, during, or after an incident belong to which mission area?
o: Mitigation
Protection
Response
Recovery
why: Mitigation reduces or eliminates risks or lessens incident effects and can be implemented before, during, or after an incident.

q: Which activity is characteristic of the recovery mission area rather than immediate response?
o: Ordering the first units to stabilize an active incident
Developing and coordinating long-term service- and site-restoration plans
Intervening to stop an incident before it occurs
Broadcasting an attack warning signal
why: Recovery includes developing, coordinating, and executing service- and site-restoration plans and reconstituting operations and services.

q: Which Disaster Response Force element operates continuously and combines fire and emergency services, security forces, and medical dispatch functions?
o: Crisis Action Team
Emergency Operations Center
Emergency Communications Center
Installation Control Center
why: The Emergency Communications Center is a 24/7 operation incorporating fire and emergency services, security forces, and medical dispatch.

q: Who has overall authority and responsibility for managing incident operations at the incident site?
o: Emergency Operations Center director
Installation commander
Command Post controller
Incident Commander
why: The Incident Commander has overall authority and responsibility for conducting and managing operations at the incident site.

q: What distinguishes first responders from emergency responders in the DAF Emergency Management Program?
o: First responders immediately act to save lives and stabilize the incident; emergency responders deploy afterward to expand Incident Commander capabilities
First responders work only at home station; emergency responders work only at deployed locations
First responders direct mission continuation; emergency responders command all on-scene operations
First responders are military personnel; emergency responders are civilian personnel
why: First responders immediately save lives, stabilize the incident, and prevent further damage; emergency responders follow to expand IC capabilities and support functions.

q: What is the installation Emergency Operations Center's primary function?
o: Exercise tactical command over all personnel at the incident site
Address imminent or realized threats and coordinate support to incident command, on-scene personnel, or other EOCs
Replace the Command Post during routine operations
Focus exclusively on long-term mission continuation priorities
why: The EOC addresses imminent or realized threats and hazards and coordinates support to incident command, on-scene personnel, and other EOCs.

q: Which statement correctly describes the installation Crisis Action Team?
o: It is the on-scene element that develops incident tactics and releases resources
It performs only emergency dispatch and alarm monitoring
It supports the commander by assessing the situation, setting mission priorities, and directing subordinate units
It manages the incident itself rather than mission continuation
why: The CAT supports the installation commander through assessment, mission prioritization, and direction of subordinate units; it focuses on mission continuation, not incident management.

q: A hazardous materials release caused by malfunctioning equipment or human error in controlling technology is classified as what type of hazard?
o: Natural disaster
Chemical warfare agent
Radiological event only
Technological hazard
why: Technological hazards are man-made events caused by a technological structure malfunction or human error in controlling technology.

q: Why do nerve and blister agents pose a primary chemical threat to air bases?
o: Their persistent nature can leave a continuing hazard
They can be delivered only by aircraft
They produce only delayed psychological effects
Standard fire extinguishers spread them
why: AFH 1 identifies nerve and blister agents as a primary air-base threat because of their persistent nature.

q: Which feature can make recognition of a biological attack difficult immediately after exposure?
o: Biological agents exist only as dry powders
Symptoms may not appear until after an agent-specific incubation period
Biological agents affect materiel but not living organisms
All biological agents have the same exposure period
why: Symptoms may not be experienced immediately, and each biological agent has a different incubation period before infection.

q: How does ionizing radiation differ from nonionizing radiation?
o: Ionizing radiation produces heat but cannot alter matter
Ionizing radiation occurs only after a nuclear detonation
Ionizing radiation has enough energy to produce ions when interacting with matter
Ionizing radiation cannot affect human cells
why: Ionizing radiation has sufficient energy to produce ions when it interacts with matter, including the human body.

q: What is the most important immediate action during a toxic industrial material incident, when feasible?
o: Put on the military protective mask and remain at the release point
Approach the source from downwind to identify it
Wait for symptoms before acting
Evacuate to an area outside the hazard's path
why: The text directs immediate evacuation outside the hazard's path when feasible; if evacuation is impractical, personnel shelter in place.

q: Which limitation must personnel remember when responding to toxic industrial materials?
o: The protective mask, ensemble, and standard collective-protection filters are not designed to protect against toxic industrial materials
Shelter-in-place is prohibited for all toxic industrial material incidents
Toxic industrial materials present only skin-contact hazards
Evacuation is permitted only after the material is identified
why: Military protective masks, ensembles, and standard collective-protection filters are not designed for protection from toxic industrial materials.

q: What does a three-to-five-minute steady tone indicate?
o: An attack or hostile act is imminent or in progress
A disaster or incident is imminent or in progress
An active shooter has been neutralized
The installation has returned to normal readiness
why: A three-to-five-minute steady tone signals that a disaster or incident is imminent or in progress.

q: What does a three-to-five-minute wavering tone direct personnel to recognize?
o: A natural disaster has ended
Recovery operations are complete
An attack or hostile act is imminent or in progress
Only a communications test is underway
why: The wavering tone signals an imminent or ongoing attack or hostile act; personnel execute security measures and follow instructions.

q: Personnel hear the announcement, “Lockdown, lockdown, lockdown.” What should they do?
o: Evacuate by the nearest exterior route regardless of conditions
Report to the Emergency Operations Center
Resume operations under normal wartime conditions
Remain calm and implement lockdown procedures
why: The repeated lockdown announcement indicates an active shooter incident; personnel remain calm and implement lockdown procedures.

q: During a shelter-in-place order for a technological disaster, which action may be required?
o: Move to a predesignated room, shut off HVAC, and cover vents and doors with plastic
Open windows to equalize air pressure
Assemble outdoors for accountability
Enter the nearest vehicle and start its ventilation system
why: Technological-disaster sheltering may require a predesignated room, shutting off HVAC, and covering vents and doors with plastic.

q: What is the purpose of risk management as a decision-making process?
o: To eliminate every possible risk before any mission begins
To evaluate courses of action, identify risks and benefits, and choose the best course for the situation
To transfer all risk decisions to safety professionals
To document mishaps only after they occur
why: Risk management systematically evaluates courses of action, identifies risks and benefits, and determines the best course for a given situation.

q: Which risk management principle provides the greatest opportunity to make informed decisions and establish effective controls?
o: Avoid every high-risk mission
Delegate risk acceptance to the lowest rank
Integrate risk management into operations and planning at all levels as early as possible
Apply risk management only after execution begins
why: Early integration into planning at every level gives the greatest opportunity for informed decisions and effective controls.

q: At what point are deliberate and real-time risk management separated?
o: When a risk rises above the low category
When a supervisor delegates control implementation
When an after-action review begins
When planning transitions to execution of the mission or activity
why: The two levels are interrelated and separate only when planning transitions to mission or activity execution.

q: Which three stages form a complete situational-awareness assessment in real-time risk management?
o: Perception of events, integration of information and goals, and projection into the future
Hazard reporting, commander approval, and formal testing
Detection, warning, and recovery
Planning, budgeting, and inspection
why: Real-time assessment uses perception of what is happening, integration of information and goals, and projection into the future.

q: What must occur when any Airman or Guardian calls “Knock-it-off” or “Timeout” during an activity?
o: Only the caller stops while the rest of the team continues
Current actions immediately halt and the situation is stabilized so the concern can be evaluated
The call takes effect only after command approval
The activity is permanently terminated without reassessment
why: Either call immediately halts current actions and requires stabilization to a safe position for evaluation; command authority cannot override it.

q: What is the goal of integrated defense?
o: To eliminate every natural hazard within the installation perimeter
To transfer installation security to local authorities
To neutralize security threats within the base boundary and base security zone so USAF operations remain unhindered
To restrict defense planning to security forces personnel
why: Integrated defense seeks to neutralize threats within the base boundary and base security zone to ensure unhindered USAF operations.

q: Which statement about a base boundary is correct?
o: It always follows the legal property line
It is identical to the installation's fenced perimeter
It includes only terrain owned by the Department of Defense
It delineates the surface area used to coordinate and deconflict operations and need not match the fenced perimeter or legal boundary
why: The base boundary facilitates coordination and deconfliction and may differ from fenced perimeters, property lines, and legal boundaries.

q: What area does the USAF planning term “base security zone” describe?
o: The area outside the base perimeter from which standoff weapons or waterborne threats could make the base vulnerable
Only the controlled areas located inside the installation fence
The airspace directly above the installation runway
The legal property contained within the base boundary
why: The base security zone is the area outside the perimeter from which standoff weapons and waterborne threats may endanger the base.

q: Which integrated defense effect uses barriers, obstacles, technology, physical security measures, and forces to slow an adversary?
o: Assess
Delay
Warn
Recover
why: Delay uses layered barriers, obstacles, technology, security measures, and forces—defense in depth—to slow adversaries.

q: In the example progression of integrated defense effects, what follows detection of a threat?
o: Immediate recovery
Automatic mission termination
Assessment by friendly forces
Removal of all barriers
why: The example progression moves from deterrence to detection, then assessment, warning, defeat, delay, defense, and recovery as needed.

q: What is the Base Defense Operations Center?
o: The installation office responsible only for security-clearance adjudication
A temporary dispatch function used only during deployments
The center that publishes antiterrorism travel advisories
The command-and-control center for integrated defense during routine and emergency operations
why: The BDOC is the integrated defense command-and-control center in both routine and emergency operations.

q: Loss or compromise of which protection-level resource would cause significant degradation to U.S. warfighting capability?
o: Protection Level 2
Protection Level 1
Protection Level 3
Protection Level 4
why: PL2 covers resources whose loss or compromise would significantly degrade U.S. warfighting capability.

q: How are Protection Level 4 resources principally secured?
o: By assigning them the maximum deterrence required for nuclear weapons
By placing them in controlled areas under owner or user security, with security forces responding to threats
By maintaining a dedicated armed escort at all times
By treating every PL4 resource as a one-of-a-kind strategic system
why: PL4 resources are contained in controlled areas, owners or users are responsible for security, and security forces respond to threats.

q: What is the correct order of the operations security cycle?
o: Assess risk, identify critical information, apply countermeasures, analyze vulnerabilities, analyze threats
Analyze threats, assess risk, identify critical information, apply countermeasures, analyze vulnerabilities
Identify critical information, analyze threats, analyze vulnerabilities, assess risk, apply countermeasures
Identify vulnerabilities, apply countermeasures, analyze threats, assess risk, identify critical information
why: The OPSEC cycle is identify critical information, analyze threats, analyze vulnerabilities, assess risk, and apply countermeasures.

q: Which operations security indicator characteristic is the sum of an activity's signatures and associations?
o: Contrast
Exposure
Signature
Profile
why: An activity's profile is the combined set of its signatures and associations.

q: An observable difference between an activity's standard profile and its current actions is what type of OPSEC indicator characteristic?
o: Contrast
Association
Exposure
Signature
why: A contrast is a difference between an activity's standard profile and its recent or current actions.

q: Unauthorized disclosure reasonably expected to cause damage—not serious or exceptionally grave damage—to national security corresponds to which classification?
o: Secret
Confidential
Top Secret
Controlled Unclassified Information
why: Confidential applies when unauthorized disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause damage to national security.

q: Who may make an original classification decision?
o: Any cleared member with annual refresher training
Any supervisor with a need to know
Only an official designated in writing
Only the author of the information
why: Only officials designated in writing may make original classification decisions.

q: Which form records end-of-day security checks in an area where classified information is used or stored?
o: SF 312
SF 703
SF 705
SF 701
why: SF 701, Activity Security Checklist, records required end-of-day checks in areas using or storing classified information.

q: What must a person do upon finding classified material out of proper control?
o: Take custody, safeguard it, and immediately notify the commander, supervisor, or security manager
Leave it untouched and notify coworkers at the end of the duty day
Destroy it immediately without documenting the event
Post a public notice asking its owner to retrieve it
why: Anyone finding uncontrolled classified material must take custody, safeguard it, and immediately notify appropriate leadership or security personnel.

q: How is a classified data spill handled before an inquiry determines whether unauthorized disclosure occurred?
o: As an infraction requiring no inquiry
As a possible compromise of classified information
As a routine computer malfunction
As a loss only if the source file cannot be found
why: A classified data spill is treated as a possible compromise until an inquiry determines whether unauthorized disclosure occurred.

q: When must a Privacy Act statement be provided?
o: Whenever an employee views any federal record
Only when classified information is collected
When individuals are asked to provide personal information about themselves for a system of records
Only after a personally identifiable information breach
why: A Privacy Act statement is required when individuals provide personal information about themselves for collection in a system of records.

q: What is the standard Freedom of Information Act time limit to deny a request or release the requested records?
o: 10 calendar days
15 workdays
30 calendar days
20 workdays
why: FOIA imposes a 20-workday limit to deny or release records, with a possible 10-workday extension for specified unusual circumstances.

q: Which sequence lists the five functions of the USAF Cybersecurity Program?
o: Identify, protect, detect, respond, recover
Prevent, classify, encrypt, transmit, destroy
Assess, authorize, monitor, inspect, report
Plan, acquire, operate, defend, retire
why: The five cybersecurity functions are Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover.

q: What is the required reaction after notification of a virus or malware detection?
o: Attempt to remove it without reporting the event
Immediately notify the information system security officer and follow local procedures
Continue operating until the system fails
Report it only if classified information was stored on the system
why: The reaction step requires immediate notification of the information system security officer and compliance with local procedures.

q: What is the consequence of using public computing facilities to access web-based government services?
o: It is permitted if no files are downloaded
It is limited authorized personal use
It constitutes compromise of login credentials and must be reported as a security incident
It is allowed when multifactor authentication is used
why: Accessing web-based government services through public computing facilities compromises login credentials and must be reported.

q: What is the objective of TEMPEST?
o: To detect malicious software by behavioral analysis
To secure classified material during registered-mail transport
To control physical entry into all installation facilities
To deny access to information that could be derived from compromising emanations within an inspectable space
why: TEMPEST measures deny unauthorized access to information obtainable by intercepting and analyzing compromising emanations.

q: What is AFOSI's antiterrorism and force-protection role?
o: It is the lead USAF agency for collection, investigation, analysis, and response to terrorist, criminal, foreign-intelligence, and security-service threats
It establishes every installation's base boundary
It approves all mobile computing devices
It serves only as the local liaison for natural disasters
why: AFOSI leads USAF collection, investigation, analysis, and response for terrorist, criminal, foreign-intelligence, and security-service threats.

q: Why are the times, locations, and durations of random antiterrorism measures regularly changed?
o: To eliminate the need for installation antiterrorism plans
To introduce uncertainty, defeat surveillance, and prevent terrorists from predicting actions
To restrict participation to security forces
To apply the measures only during FPCON Charlie
why: Changing random measures creates uncertainty, frustrates surveillance, and makes installation actions difficult to predict.

q: By when must an individual report a reportable contact or reportable information to AFOSI?
o: At the next annual counterintelligence briefing
Within 90 days after returning to home station
Immediately, defined as within 30 days of the contact
Only after confirming foreign-intelligence involvement
why: AFI 71-101, Volume 4 requires immediate reporting—within 30 days of contact—verbally or in writing to AFOSI.

q: What do DAF Instructions, Air Force Instructions, and Space Force Instructions generally tell readers?
o: Why a historical event occurred
How to perform specialized technical procedures step by step
Which optional reference aids may be ignored
What to do by directing action and standardizing compliance across the DAF
why: DAFIs, AFIs, and SPFIs generally direct what to do and standardize compliant actions across the Department.

q: What do DAF, Air Force, and Space Force manuals generally provide?
o: How-to procedures and detailed technical guidance for standard tasks or education and training
Only nonmandatory historical background
Policy statements that may never contain procedures
Rules issued exclusively by combatant commanders
why: Manuals generally provide how-to detail, technical procedures, or support for education and training programs.

q: How should Airmen treat guidance in a nondirective publication?
o: It is legally binding in every circumstance
Compliance is expected but not mandatory, and guidance may be adapted to circumstances
It may be used only by publication managers
It supersedes all directive publications
why: Nondirective publications are reference aids whose guidance may be modified; compliance is expected but not mandatory.

q: When may a competent authority require an Airman to report for duty?
o: Only during the published duty day
Only after leave has formally ended
At any time and location, including weekends, holidays, and while on leave, for as long as necessary
Only at the Airman's permanent duty station
why: Airmen are always subject to duty and, when properly directed, must report at any time and location for as long as necessary.

q: What consequences may follow failure to comply with a General Order?
o: Only verbal counseling
Automatic discharge without proceedings
Civil liability but no military action
Adverse administrative action, nonjudicial punishment, or UCMJ criminal prosecution
why: Failure to obey General Orders can lead to administrative action, nonjudicial punishment, or criminal prosecution under the UCMJ.

q: What is a central humanitarian purpose of the law of war?
o: To lessen conflict's effects, prevent unnecessary suffering, and protect combatants and noncombatants
To prohibit every use of military force
To replace commanders' operational judgment with civilian courts
To protect only military prisoners of war
why: The law of war seeks to lessen conflict's effects, protect combatants and noncombatants, and prevent unnecessary suffering.

q: How is law-of-war training assigned to USAF personnel?
o: Every member receives an identical course regardless of duties
Training is commensurate with duties and responsibilities, with specialized training for groups facing unique situations
Only aircrews, medical personnel, and security forces receive training
Training is required only before deployment to international armed conflict
why: Training matches members' duties and responsibilities; groups such as aircrews, medics, and security forces receive specialized instruction.

q: What does the law-of-war principle of military necessity permit?
o: Any action that shortens a conflict
Attacks on civilians when they may influence enemy morale
Measures needed to defeat the enemy efficiently that are not prohibited by the law of war
Reprisals against all protected persons
why: Military necessity allows measures needed for efficient defeat of the enemy only when those measures are not prohibited by the law of war.

q: Which principle forbids suffering, injury, or destruction unnecessary to achieve a legitimate military purpose?
o: Distinction
Honor
Proportionality
Humanity
why: Humanity prohibits suffering, injury, or destruction beyond what is necessary for a legitimate military purpose.

q: A civilian school is being used to make an effective contribution to military action. What may happen to its status under the principle of distinction?
o: It may lose its protected civilian-object status
It remains absolutely immune from attack in every circumstance
It automatically becomes a prisoner-of-war facility
It may be attacked without considering proportionality
why: A civilian object can lose protected status if used to make an effective contribution to military action, though other law-of-war rules still apply.

q: What does proportionality require when planning an otherwise justified attack?
o: That an attack cause no incidental civilian harm whatsoever
That expected incidental harm not be excessive relative to the anticipated concrete and direct military advantage
That civilian harm equal the value of the target
That only weapons producing no blast effect be used
why: Proportionality bars attacks with expected incidental harm excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

q: Which conduct is prohibited by the law-of-war principle of honor?
o: A lawful ruse intended to mislead the enemy
Camouflage used to conceal a military position
Killing or wounding an enemy through perfidy or treachery
Withholding operational plans from the enemy
why: Honor prohibits breaches of trust such as killing or wounding through perfidy, while lawful ruses remain permitted.

q: How must a captured person be treated while doubt remains about whether the person is a lawful combatant, noncombatant, or unprivileged belligerent?
o: As a civilian criminal with no law-of-war protection
According to the captor's preferred classification
As an unprivileged belligerent until the person proves otherwise
With Geneva Prisoner of War Convention protections until status is determined
why: A captured individual of uncertain status receives Geneva POW Convention protections until actual status is determined.

q: Which military personnel are examples of noncombatants who may not be made the object of attack?
o: Permanent medical and religious personnel not authorized to engage in combatant activities
All military intelligence personnel
Every member assigned to a headquarters
Combatants who temporarily remove their uniforms
why: Permanent medical and religious personnel are military noncombatants who must be respected and protected from attack.

q: What happens to civilians who take an active or direct part in hostilities?
o: They automatically gain lawful combatant immunity
They forfeit protection from being made the object of attack while participating
They must be treated as permanent medical personnel
They retain absolute protection from direct attack
why: Civilians directly participating in hostilities forfeit their protection from being made the object of attack.

q: When may an airman parachuting from a disabled enemy aircraft be attacked?
o: Whenever the parachute is visible
Only before leaving the aircraft
If the airman resists while descending or lands behind friendly lines and continues fighting
Never, even if the airman continues hostile acts
why: An airman offering no resistance during descent may not be attacked, but resistance in descent or continued fighting after landing can make the person subject to attack.

q: What duty accompanies every service member's obligation to comply with the law of war?
o: Obey every order without evaluating its legality
Report suspected violations only after obtaining proof beyond doubt
Refer every targeting decision directly to an international tribunal
Refuse clearly illegal orders to commit law-of-war violations
why: The duty to comply includes refusing clearly illegal orders to commit law-of-war violations.

q: If a suspected law-of-war violation may involve a U.S. commander, where should the report be made?
o: To the next higher U.S. command authority
Only to the commander named in the allegation
Directly to the foreign government involved
Only to civilian law enforcement
why: When an allegation involves or may involve a U.S. commander, it should be reported to the next higher U.S. command authority.

q: What do rules of engagement generally establish?
o: The standards for granting security clearances
Parameters for when, where, how, why, and against whom force may be used
The order of succession among prisoners of war
The publication process for military manuals
why: ROE set the parameters governing when, where, how, why, and against whom commanders and Airmen may use force.

q: When should forces committing hostile acts or demonstrating hostile intent be warned and allowed to withdraw or cease?
o: Only after force has already been used
Whenever the opposing force requests negotiations
When time and circumstances permit
Only when ordered by the President
why: De-escalation calls for warning and an opportunity to withdraw or cease threatening actions when time and circumstances permit.

q: Under rules of engagement, what limits force used in self-defense?
o: It must always be less than the force threatened
It may continue until every potential threat is removed
It is limited to nonlethal measures
It must be necessary and reasonable in nature, duration, and scope compared with the threat
why: Self-defense force must be necessary to counter the threat and reasonable in nature, duration, and scope based on facts known at the time.

q: Who receives Level A Code of Conduct training?
o: All members of the U.S. Armed Forces during entry training
Only members at moderate risk of capture
Only aircrews and special mission forces
Only personnel exposed to classified information
why: Level A is the minimum understanding required for all Armed Forces members and is given during entry training.

q: Which members require Level C Code of Conduct training?
o: Members whose duties carry no meaningful capture risk
Members at significant or high risk of capture who are especially vulnerable to exploitation because of position, rank, or seniority
All civilian employees during initial orientation
Only prisoners after repatriation
why: Level C applies to high- or significant-capture-risk members whose position, rank, or seniority creates greater-than-average exploitation risk.

q: Under Code of Conduct Article III, how should a prisoner of war treat parole or special favors from the enemy?
o: Accept them if they improve personal survival odds
Accept parole but refuse material favors
Accept neither parole nor special favors
Accept them only with another prisoner's approval
why: Article III requires continued resistance and expressly states that prisoners will accept neither parole nor special favors from the enemy.

q: During a rescue attempt in a terrorist-hostage situation, what should a hostage do?
o: Run toward rescuers and identify the captors
Attempt to disarm a captor while rescuers enter
Argue with captors to distract them
Take cover, remain stationary when practicable, and do not try to help rescuers
why: During rescue, hostages should take cover, remain stationary when practicable, and avoid attempting to help the rescuers.

q: Which statement best describes the Air Force Inspection System (AFIS)?
o: A disciplinary process used only after a unit fails an inspection
A credible, independent assessment process commanders use to measure assigned-force capabilities
A self-assessment database used exclusively by shop-level personnel
A scheduling system for eliminating all external inspections
why: AFIS gives commanders a credible, independent process for assessing the capabilities of assigned forces.

q: To whom does The Inspector General communicate directly on Department of the Air Force IG matters?
o: Only the Secretary of Defense
Only MAJCOM commanders and wing inspectors general
The SecAF, Chief of Staff of the Air Force, Chief of Space Operations, and other USAF and USSF command elements
Congressional committees and state governors
why: TIG communicates directly with the SecAF, CSAF, CSO, and all other USAF and USSF command elements on IG matters.

q: Which task belongs to Wing, Delta, and equivalent inspectors general?
o: Approve all unit disciplinary actions
Command the units being inspected
Replace commanders' responsibility for readiness evaluations
Execute the commander's inspection program and validate unit self-assessments
why: Wing, Delta, and equivalent IGs execute the CCIP, validate and verify self-assessments, and independently assess unit effectiveness.

q: What authority do inspection Gatekeepers exercise on behalf of their commanders?
o: They may approve, disapprove, schedule, deconflict, and eliminate duplication among inspection-type activities
They may waive compliance requirements identified during inspections
They may replace a Unit Effectiveness Inspection with a self-assessment
They may direct non-mission-essential activities to take precedence over commander priorities
why: Gatekeepers synchronize inspection activity and may approve, disapprove, schedule, deconflict, and eliminate duplication.

q: What is the purpose of the Commander's Inspection Program at the Wing level?
o: To certify every nuclear-capable unit
To improve readiness, efficiency, discipline, effectiveness, compliance, and surety
To replace all MAJCOM external evaluations
To determine individual promotion eligibility
why: The CCIP improves readiness, efficiency, discipline, effectiveness, compliance, and surety at the Wing level.

q: A Nuclear Surety Inspection evaluates whether a certified nuclear-capable unit can do what?
o: Schedule non-Air Force inspection requirements
Eliminate all risk associated with nuclear operations
Manage assigned nuclear resources and execute nuclear missions safely, securely, and reliably
Conduct a multi-year evaluation of all four Major Graded Areas
why: An NSI evaluates safe, secure, and reliable management of nuclear resources and execution of nuclear missions.

q: Which list contains the four Major Graded Areas used in a Unit Effectiveness Inspection?
o: Policy, training, manpower, and facilities
Readiness, compliance, discipline, and surety
Planning, organizing, directing, and controlling
Managing resources, leading people, improving the unit, and executing the mission
why: The UEI's four MGAs are managing resources, leading people, improving the unit, and executing the mission.

q: What is the primary purpose of the Unit Self-Assessment Program?
o: To accurately identify and report issues so Airmen can safely report what is true
To prepare units to conceal deficiencies before an external inspection
To transfer compliance responsibility from commanders to inspectors
To score individual Airmen against Major Graded Areas
why: The USAP is intended to identify and report issues accurately in a climate where Airmen can safely report the truth.

q: What is the Management Internal Control Toolset (MICT)?
o: The system used to schedule nuclear inspections
A USAF program of record and tool for managing Unit Self-Assessment Programs
A complaint channel available only to commanders
The database used solely for final inspection reports
why: MICT is a USAF program of record used to manage USAPs.

q: After an inspection, validated report data must be categorized in which three ways?
o: Open, pending, or closed
Minor, major, or critical
Strengths, deficiencies, or recommended improvement areas
Compliant, noncompliant, or exempt
why: Inspection reports categorize validated data as strengths, deficiencies, or recommended improvement areas.

q: Which statement about communicating with an Inspector General or member of Congress is correct?
o: A supervisor may restrict the communication until local remedies are exhausted
The communication must be submitted only in writing
Only complaints involving fraud, waste, or abuse may bypass the chain of command
No person may restrict a military member from making a lawful communication to an IG or member of Congress
why: Public law prohibits restricting a military member's lawful communication to an IG or member of Congress.

q: Who may investigate allegations of reprisal and restriction under the Military Whistleblower's Protection Act?
o: Only the Inspector General
Any commander in the complainant's chain
The Equal Opportunity office
The Staff Judge Advocate without an IG referral
why: Only the IG may investigate reprisal and restriction allegations under the Military Whistleblower's Protection Act.

q: What must an Airman requesting a religious accommodation do while the request is pending?
o: Suspend compliance with the affected directive
Continue complying with directives, instructions, and lawful orders until approval
Treat submission of the request as temporary approval
Comply only if the commander issues a separate written order
why: Requesters must continue to comply with directives, instructions, and lawful orders until the accommodation is approved.

q: If a religious accommodation is denied, what standard must the decision satisfy?
o: It must be based solely on local custom
It must show that any restriction is administratively convenient
It must directly relate to a compelling government interest and use the least restrictive means necessary
It must establish that the belief is shared by a recognized religious organization
why: A denial must be fact-based, tied to a compelling military interest, and use the least restrictive means necessary.

q: Which political activity is prohibited for a USAF member, whether in uniform or not?
o: Voting in an election
Privately expressing a political opinion
Attending a rally solely as a spectator while out of uniform
Participating in partisan fundraising, campaign management, rallies, conventions, or debates
why: Members may not participate in specified partisan activities, regardless of uniform wear or apparent official endorsement.

q: After receiving an allegation of activity prohibited by DoDI 1325.06, when must military organizations normally report it to the servicing IG?
o: Within 30 calendar days; Reserve Component officials have 60 calendar days
Within 15 duty days for every component
Within 60 calendar days; Reserve Component officials have 30 calendar days
Only after an investigation substantiates the allegation
why: The normal deadline is 30 calendar days; Reserve Component officials must transmit within 60 calendar days.

q: How does AFH 1 distinguish the two blood alcohol concentration thresholds discussed for impairment?
o: A BAC of 0.05 is conclusive impairment, while 0.08 requires other evidence
Above 0.08 is considered impaired; 0.05 to less than 0.08 may support a presumption of impairment
Only a BAC above 0.10 can establish impairment
Both thresholds automatically require permanent loss of installation driving privileges
why: A BAC greater than .08 is considered impaired; from .05 to less than .08, impairment may be presumed with other competent evidence.

q: Why should commander-directed drug testing be used only as a last resort?
o: It requires approval from a military judge
It can test only officers
Its results may not be used for UCMJ discipline or to characterize an administrative discharge
It is valid only when the member voluntarily consents
why: Commander-directed test results cannot support UCMJ discipline or characterize an administrative discharge.

q: Which statement describes a probable-cause urine search under Military Rule of Evidence 315?
o: It may be ordered without authorization whenever a unit inspection is announced
It may be based only on a member's refusal to consent
Its results may be used only for medical referral
It requires authorization from competent search authority and a reasonable belief that evidence of illegal drug use will be found
why: A probable-cause search requires proper authorization and a reasonable belief that evidence of illegal drug use will be found.

q: How may a commander use a qualifying member's voluntary self-identification of a substance-use problem?
o: It may not be used against the member under the UCMJ or to characterize service in an administrative discharge
It automatically requires an under other than honorable discharge
It may be used as proof of misconduct without corroboration
It bars the member from receiving an ADAPT assessment
why: Qualifying voluntary self-identification is protected from use in UCMJ action and discharge characterization decisions.

q: Which list contains all six forms of harassment covered by the Air Force Equal Opportunity Program?
o: Verbal, written, physical, electronic, visual, and social
Discriminatory, sexual, bullying, hazing, retaliation, and reprisal
Coercion, intimidation, favoritism, reprisal, assault, and neglect
Bullying, hazing, fraternization, reprisal, misconduct, and discrimination
why: The six forms are discriminatory harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, hazing, retaliation, and reprisal.

q: Can a service member be responsible for bullying or hazing if the victim actually or implicitly consented?
o: No; consent is a complete defense
Only when the victim is junior in rank
Yes; consent does not prevent responsibility, regardless of the victim's grade, status, or service
Yes, but only at official unit functions
why: A member may be responsible despite actual or implied consent and regardless of the victim's grade, rank, status, or service.

q: Which rule applies to military Equal Opportunity complaints?
o: Any coworker may file on behalf of the affected member
Only commanders may initiate a complaint
The EO office accepts complaints arising from off-base civilian employment
The filer must be the subject of the alleged discrimination or sexual harassment; third parties cannot file for another person
why: Military EO complaints must be filed by the affected individual; third parties are referred to their chain of command.

q: What is the normal initial duration of placement on a control roster?
o: Six months, with possible early removal at the commander's discretion
One year with no early-removal authority
Three duty days beginning when the member acknowledges the action
Ninety days beginning when the commander assumes command
why: Control-roster placement initially lasts six months, although the commander may remove it early.

q: Which former USAF member may request Air Force Discharge Review Board review within 15 years of separation?
o: A member dismissed by general court-martial
A member with an administrative discharge, but not one with a bad-conduct discharge, dishonorable discharge, or general court-martial dismissal
Only a retiree seeking to change a reenlistment code
Any former member, with no exception for the type of discharge
why: The board reviews eligible discharges within 15 years, excluding bad-conduct and dishonorable discharges and dismissal by general court-martial.

q: What is the goal of the Physical Fitness Program?
o: To prepare Airmen only during the month before an assessment
To measure body composition without considering conditioning
To motivate year-round conditioning emphasizing aerobic conditioning, muscular fitness, and healthy eating
To establish one identical fitness score standard for every age and gender
why: The PFP promotes year-round physical conditioning built around aerobic conditioning, muscular fitness, and healthy eating.

q: How does the Body Composition Program assess Air Force members?
o: It uses body weight alone during each fitness assessment
It uses abdominal circumference as a scored fitness component
It calculates body-fat percentage from age and weight
It requires an annual assessment in the member's birth month and uses waist circumference divided by height
why: The annual BCA occurs in the birth month and calculates waist-to-height ratio by dividing waist circumference by height.

q: Which waist-to-height ratio is classified as meeting the Body Composition Program standard?
o: A ratio below 0.55
A ratio of 0.55 or higher
Any ratio below 0.75
A ratio above 0.55 when the fitness score is satisfactory
why: A WHtR below 0.55 meets the standard and is categorized as low-moderate risk.

q: What is the required sequence for fitness assessment components?
o: Cardiorespiratory, core endurance, muscular strength, then height and weight
Height and weight, muscular strength, core endurance, then cardiorespiratory fitness
Muscular strength, cardiorespiratory fitness, height and weight, then core endurance
Core endurance, height and weight, cardiorespiratory fitness, then muscular strength
why: The sequence is height and weight first, followed by muscular strength, core endurance, and cardiorespiratory fitness.

q: Which timing rule applies to a fitness assessment?
o: Components may be spread over two duty days
The assessment must finish within one hour with no required rest
All components must be completed the same day within three hours, with at least five minutes between components
Only the aerobic and muscular components must occur on the same day
why: All components occur within a three-hour window on one day, with a minimum five-minute rest between components.

q: How are the 100 possible fitness assessment points allocated?
o: 40 aerobic, 30 muscular, and 30 core endurance
50 aerobic, 25 muscular, and 25 core endurance
60 aerobic and 40 body composition
60 aerobic, 20 muscular, and 20 core endurance
why: The maximums are 60 points for aerobic fitness, 20 for muscular fitness, and 20 for core endurance.

q: Why does meeting every minimum component score not necessarily produce a passing assessment?
o: The minimum values together do not generate the required composite score of 75 or greater
A member must score excellent in at least one component
Body composition must add at least 10 points
Each component must independently earn 75 percent
why: Minimum performance in every component still may total less than the passing composite score of 75.

q: How do medical component exemptions affect fitness testing?
o: Any exemption cancels the entire assessment
Airmen still test on every component not specifically exempted by the medical profile
Only the aerobic component may be exempted
An exemption may be granted without a medical-provider recommendation
why: A medical profile exempts only specified components; the Airman must complete all non-exempt components.

q: What is muscular endurance?
o: The maximum force produced in one effort
The ability to sustain large-muscle aerobic exercise
The ability of a muscle group to repeat contractions long enough to cause muscular fatigue
The maximum range through which a joint can move
why: Muscular endurance is repeated muscle-group contraction over sufficient time to cause fatigue.

q: How does AFH 1 define aerobic fitness?
o: The force generated by a muscle group in one contraction
The ability to recover after resistance training
The ability to maintain flexibility under load
The ability to perform large-muscle, dynamic, moderate-to-high intensity exercise for prolonged periods
why: Aerobic fitness is cardiorespiratory endurance during prolonged, dynamic, large-muscle exercise at moderate-to-high intensity.

q: What is the recommended duration of a dynamic warm-up before vigorous exercise?
o: Five to seven minutes
One to two minutes
Ten to fifteen minutes of static stretching only
At least thirty minutes
why: A five-to-seven-minute dynamic warm-up increases blood flow and range of motion while reducing injury risk.

q: What is a principal purpose of a post-workout cool-down?
o: To immediately stop circulation to active muscles
To reduce activity gradually, prevent blood pooling, hasten recovery, and avoid injury
To raise the heart rate before stretching
To replace the need for rehydration
why: A cool-down gradually reduces activity to prevent blood pooling, aid recovery, and reduce injury risk.

q: In nutrition and fitness planning, what does SMART stand for?
o: Simple, Motivating, Active, Realistic, Trackable
Specific, Managed, Accurate, Repeatable, Timed
Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Timely
Sustainable, Measured, Achievable, Resilient, and Tested
why: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Attainable, Relevant, and Timely.

q: What carbohydrate-to-protein ratio is identified as optimal for a post-recovery beverage or snack?
o: One-to-one
Two-to-one
Three-to-one
Four-to-one
why: The recommended post-recovery ratio is four grams of carbohydrate for every gram of protein.

q: What proportion of total daily caloric intake is generally recommended from carbohydrates?
o: 45 to 65 percent
10 to 20 percent
20 to 35 percent
70 to 85 percent
why: The general recommendation is for carbohydrates to provide 45 to 65 percent of daily calories.

q: How does recommended daily fiber intake compare with average American intake?
o: Both are about 12 to 15 grams
The recommendation is 20 to 35 grams, compared with an average intake of 12 to 15 grams
The recommendation is 45 to 65 grams, compared with an average of 20 to 35 grams
The recommendation is lower than average intake
why: Average intake is 12-15 grams per day, while 20-35 grams is recommended.

q: What daily sodium limit do the Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend for most adults?
o: 1,000 milligrams
1,500 milligrams for every adult
2,300 milligrams, about one teaspoon of table salt
3,400 milligrams, matching average consumption
why: Most adults should limit sodium to 2,300 milligrams per day, roughly one teaspoon of table salt.

q: Why should Airmen look for third-party verification when buying dietary supplements?
o: Third parties guarantee the supplement will improve performance
Military policy prohibits every supplement without third-party approval
Verification makes consultation with a flight surgeon unnecessary
The FDA does not test supplements before sale, so third-party labels can indicate testing for purity or quality
why: Because the FDA does not test supplements before sale, third-party certification can provide evidence of purity or quality testing.

q: What total daily water consumption is generally identified for women and men, respectively?
o: 2.7 liters for women and 3.7 liters for men
1.5 liters for women and 2.0 liters for men
3.7 liters for women and 2.7 liters for men
Six liters for each
why: General total daily consumption from water, beverages, and food is 2.7 liters for women and 3.7 liters for men.

q: What upper fluid-intake limits does AFH 1 suggest to reduce over-hydration risk?
